knowledge_statements.title: Exact Subgradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact first-order oracle for a proper convex objective at points admitting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. An exact subgradient oracle accepts any valid query \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) for which \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\), and returns \((f(x),g_x)\) with \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\); equivalently, \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in X.\] If only first-order information is requested, the value component may be omitted, but the returned vector must still satisfy the displayed inequality without error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every valid query point having a nonempty subdifferential, an exact oracle returns a true subgradient, optionally together with the exact function value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\) for every valid query \(x\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x

children.title: Approximate Subgradient Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Oracle access characterized by controlled approximation of subgradient information.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Subgradient Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise approximation of an exact subgradient at the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a finite-dimensional normed space \(X\), and fix \(\rho\ge0\). A \(\rho\)-approximate subgradient oracle returns, at each \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), a vector \(\widetilde g_x\in X^*\) satisfying \[\operatorname{dist}_*\!\left(\widetilde g_x,\partial f(x)\right)\le\rho.\] Thus there exists \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\) with \(\|\widetilde g_x-g_x\|_*\le\rho\). The tolerance may depend on the query or iteration, in which case \(\rho\) is replaced by \(\rho_x\) or \(\rho_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate oracle returns a vector within a prescribed dual-norm distance of some exact subgradient at the queried point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on a finite-dimensional normed space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_*(\widetilde g_x,\partial f(x))\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: distance induced by the dual norm

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Algorithm Models and Convergence Conditions I p. 15

children.title: Inexact Subgradient Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Oracle access affected by incomplete or imperfect subgradient computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Subgradient Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error relaxation of the global subgradient inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). An \(\varepsilon\)-inexact subgradient oracle returns \(\widetilde g_x\in X^*\) satisfying \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\widetilde g_x,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }y\in X.\] Equivalently, \(\widetilde g_x\in\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)\), the \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential. An iteration-dependent oracle may use errors \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\); convergence results must separately control their interaction with the algorithmic step sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact oracle returns an epsilon-subgradient whose affine lower model may violate the exact subgradient inequality by at most an additive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g_x\in\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2.2 Basic Algorithm Models p. 18

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.2 Basic Algorithm Models p. 18

children.title: Approximation–Inexactness Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions, overlaps, and ownership boundaries between the two error sources.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation–Inexactness Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion from normwise subgradient error to additive model error on a bounded feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(C\subset\operatorname{dom}f\) be nonempty, convex, and of finite diameter \(D=\sup_{u,v\in C}\|u-v\|\). Suppose \(x\in C\), \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\), and \(\|\widetilde g_x-g_x\|_*\le\rho\) for some \(\rho\ge0\). Then, for every \(y\in C\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\widetilde g_x,y-x\rangle-\rho D.\] Hence normwise \(\rho\)-approximation implies additive inexactness \(\varepsilon=\rho D\) relative to \(C\). Without a finite uniform bound on \(\|y-x\|\), normwise error alone yields no uniform additive error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a feasible set of diameter D, dual-norm subgradient error rho yields additive oracle error at most rho D; without a uniform distance bound, no such uniform additive error follows.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
\(C\subset\operatorname{dom}f\) is nonempty, convex, and has finite diameter \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g_x\in\partial^{C}_{\rho D}f(x)\), meaning the inexact subgradient inequality holds for every \(y\in C\).

notation.meaning: diameter of the feasible set C
epsilon-subdifferential with comparison points restricted to C

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Subgradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditionally unbiased stochastic oracle with a bounded conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(\mathcal F\) be the sigma-algebra of information available before a query \(x\), where \(x\) is \(\mathcal F\)-measurable and belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}f\) almost surely. A stochastic subgradient oracle returns a random vector \(G(x,\xi)\in X^*\) such that \[\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid\mathcal F]\in\partial f(x),\qquad \mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)\|_*^2\mid\mathcal F]\le M^2\] almost surely for some finite constant \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an almost surely valid query, the stochastic oracle returns a random dual vector whose conditional mean is a true subgradient and whose conditional second moment is uniformly bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid\mathcal F]\in\partial f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)\|_*^2\mid\mathcal F]\le M^2\) almost surely.

children.title: Incremental Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Sequential access patterns that reveal limited objective information per oracle interaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential one-component-at-a-time access for a finite-sum convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x)\), where \(m\ge1\) and each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex. Incremental oracle access means that at iteration \(k\), an algorithm selects one index \(i_k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), queries only component \(f_{i_k}\) at a valid point \(x_k\), and receives a vector \(g_k\in\partial f_{i_k}(x_k)\), optionally together with \(f_{i_k}(x_k)\). Each iteration uses one component-oracle call and does not require simultaneous access to the other components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental oracle access reveals first-order information for one selected finite-sum component per iteration, without querying all components simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
\(f=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i\) with \(m\ge1\) and each \(f_i\) proper and convex.
Each valid query satisfies \(x_k\in\operatorname{dom}f_{i_k}\) and \(\partial f_{i_k}(x_k)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One incremental query returns \(g_k\in\partial f_{i_k}(x_k)\) using one component-oracle call.

notation.meaning: subgradient returned by the selected component oracle

children.title: Component Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing subgradients from identifiable objective components.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed first-order access model for finite-sum convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f_i(x)\), where \(w_i>0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1\), and each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex. A component subgradient oracle accepts \((x,i)\), where \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_i\), and \(\partial f_i(x)\ne\varnothing\), and returns \((f_i(x),g_i(x))\) with \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\). One call reveals no other component information. If \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{dom}f_i\) and one obtains \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\) for every \(i\), then \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g_i(x)\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component oracle returns the value and a subgradient of one indexed finite-sum term. Querying every component at a common valid point permits construction of a full-objective subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
\(f=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f_i\), where the weights are positive and sum to one.
A valid component query satisfies \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_i\) and \(\partial f_i(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A query returns \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\); after valid queries to every component at the same point, \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g_i(x)\in\partial f(x)\).

children.title: Component Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cyclic, randomized, prioritized, or availability-driven component selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic and randomized schedules for component-oracle queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge1\), and for every integer \(k\ge0\), let \(i_k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) denote the selected component. Standard selection regimes include: cyclic selection, \(i_k=1+(k\bmod m)\); essentially cyclic selection, for which some integer \(T\ge m\) satisfies \(\{i_k,\ldots,i_{k+T-1}\}=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) for every \(k\ge0\); and randomized selection, for which \(i_k\) is sampled conditionally on the past with \(p_{k,i}=\mathbb P(i_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)\). Uniform sampling satisfies \(p_{k,i}=1/m\), while persistent randomized coverage requires a constant \(p_{\min}>0\) such that \(p_{k,i}\ge p_{\min}\) for every \(k\ge0\) and every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component queries may use cyclic, bounded-coverage, or randomized schedules; persistent randomized coverage keeps every component's conditional selection probability uniformly positive.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_k\) is the information available before selecting \(i_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed rule defines a component-selection regime with explicit coverage or conditional-sampling requirements.

notation.meaning: conditional probability of selecting component i

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Value Subgradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-and-supergradient oracle for a concave Lagrange dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(q:Y\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) be proper and concave. A dual-value subgradient oracle accepts \(y\in\operatorname{dom}q\) and returns \((q(y),s_y)\), where \(s_y\) is a supergradient of \(q\): \[q(z)\le q(y)+\langle s_y,z-y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }z\in Y.\] Equivalently, \(-s_y\in\partial(-q)(y)\). In particular, if \(q(y)=\inf_{x\in U}\{\phi(x)+\langle y,c(x)\rangle\}\) and the infimum at \(y\) is attained by \(x_y\in U\), then the same minimizer yields the exact value \(q(y)\) and the supergradient \(s_y=c(x_y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-value oracle returns an exact concave dual value and a supergradient. For the stated Lagrangian sign convention, an attaining primal minimizer supplies the constraint-residual supergradient.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
For the Lagrangian specialization, \(q(y)=\inf_{x\in U}\{\phi(x)+\langle y,c(x)\rangle\}\) and the infimum at \(y\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(z)\le q(y)+\langle s_y,z-y\rangle\) for every \(z\in Y\); in the stated Lagrangian specialization, \(s_y=c(x_y)\).

notation.meaning: constraint-residual vector under the stated Lagrangian convention

children.title: Constraint-Access Models
children.top_down_role: Ways in which feasible geometry is exposed to nonsmooth first-order methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Domain Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained access model in which every ambient-space iterate is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Full-domain access holds when the feasible set is \(C=X\) and the first-order oracle may be queried at every \(x\in X\). Consequently, Euclidean feasibility restoration is the identity operation, \[P_C(x)=x\qquad\text{for every }x\in X,\] and a subgradient update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\) remains feasible whenever \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and \(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-domain access means every ambient-space point is feasible and queryable, so Euclidean projection is the identity and unconstrained subgradient steps remain feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in X\) is feasible and queryable, and \(P_C=I\).

source_refs.locator: 8 Primal and Dual Projected Subgradient Methods p. 195

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Primal and Dual Projected Subgradient Methods p. 195

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Projection Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint oracle returning an exact nearest feasible point in Euclidean geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Euclidean projection access means that an oracle can evaluate, for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), the uniquely defined point \[P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2.\] Its output is characterized by \[\langle z-P_C(z),x-P_C(z)\rangle\le0\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Thus a projected subgradient step can compute \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\) using one projection-oracle call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean projection access returns the unique feasible point nearest to any query and thereby implements a projected subgradient update.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(z)\) exists uniquely for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) and satisfies the projection variational inequality.

children.title: Bregman Projection Access
children.top_down_role: Constraint access through Bregman projection subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Projection Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact projection onto a convex set under a Legendre-generated Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional space, and let \(h\) be a Legendre function with \(C\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\ne\varnothing\). For \(z\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), define \(D_h(x,z)=h(x)-h(z)-\langle\nabla h(z),x-z\rangle\). Bregman projection access returns a minimizer \[P_C^h(z)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,z),\] whenever this minimum is attained. If \(h\) is strictly convex on the relevant domain, the returned minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman projection access minimizes a Legendre-generated divergence from the query point over the feasible set; strict convexity makes the projection unique.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, with \(C\cap\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C^h(z)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,z)\), uniquely when \(h\) is strictly convex on the relevant domain.

source_refs.locator: 9.1 From Projected Subgradient to Mirror Descent p. 247

children.title: Bregman Proximal Access
children.top_down_role: Access to generalized proximal subproblems using Bregman geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Proximal Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle access to a regularized convex subproblem in a chosen Bregman geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(h:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\omega\) be differentiable and strictly convex on an open set containing \(C\). Bregman proximal access means that, for every query \((x,g,\eta)\) with \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), \(g\) in the dual space, and \(\eta>0\), an oracle returns some
\[
P^{\omega}_{\eta h}(x,g)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\left\{\langle g,z\rangle+h(z)+\eta^{-1}D_{\omega}(z,x)\right\},
\]
where \(D_{\omega}(z,x)=\omega(z)-\omega(x)-\langle\nabla\omega(x),z-x\rangle\), whenever the argmin is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle solves a convex linearized-plus-regularizer subproblem stabilized by Bregman distance, for every admissible base point, dual direction, and positive stepsize.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(C\).
\(\omega\) is differentiable and strictly convex on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\omega}_{\eta h}(x,g)\) is available as a minimizer of the displayed Bregman proximal subproblem.

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the distance-generating function omega.

children.title: Projection–Prox Access Boundary
children.top_down_role: Equivalence regimes, reductions, and computational distinctions between the access models.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection–Prox Access Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact one-way reduction of Bregman projection to Bregman proximal access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\omega\) be differentiable and strictly convex on an open set containing \(C\cup\{y\}\). Define \(D_{\omega}(z,y)=\omega(z)-\omega(y)-\langle\nabla\omega(y),z-y\rangle\) and suppose the Bregman projection set is nonempty. For the extended-valued indicator \(\delta_C\), and every \(\eta>0\),
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in E}\left\{\delta_C(z)+\eta^{-1}D_{\omega}(z,y)\right\}
=
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}D_{\omega}(z,y).
\]
Thus Bregman proximal access for \(h=\delta_C\) implements Bregman projection access. A projection oracle does not, from this identity alone, implement proximal access for a general convex term \(h\); such an implementation requires a separate reduction of the proximal subproblem to an available projection problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman projection is exactly the indicator-function instance of Bregman proximal access. The reverse implementation for a general convex term requires additional problem-specific structure.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\omega\) is differentiable and strictly convex wherever the displayed Bregman divergence is evaluated.
The displayed projection argmin is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}^{\omega}_{\eta\delta_C}(y)=\Pi_C^{\omega}(y)\) as an equality of minimizer sets, while no general converse oracle reduction follows without additional structure.

notation.meaning: Extended-valued indicator of the feasible set.
Bregman projection onto the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Functional-Constraint Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order oracle model for feasibility described by convex inequality functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in X:c_j(x)\leq 0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(X\) is a known closed convex set and every \(c_j:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex. Functional-constraint access consists of an oracle which, at any query \(x\in X\), returns the values \(c_j(x)\) and subgradients \(s_j\in\partial c_j(x)\) for requested indices. The returned data provide the valid cutting planes
\[
c_j(z)\geq c_j(x)+\langle s_j,z-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }z\in X.
\]
Thus feasibility is testable from the values, and any violated constraint supplies a separating affine inequality, without requiring direct projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint values test feasibility, while a subgradient of any violated convex constraint supplies a separating cut without requiring projection onto the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a known closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A query identifies violated constraints and yields valid subgradient cuts separating the query from \(C\).

notation.meaning: Feasible region defined by convex inequalities.
A subgradient of the requested constraint at the query point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle definition and separating-cut conclusion are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but no citation supports the precise functional-constraint access model.

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive-Projection Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity boundary when exact feasibility restoration dominates first-order work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an iterative first-order method whose nominal iteration uses one objective-oracle call and one exact projection \(\Pi_C\). If objective-oracle cost is \(T_f\), projection cost is \(T_P\), and \(N(\varepsilon)\) iterations ensure accuracy \(\varepsilon\), then its total primitive-operation cost is at least
\[
N(\varepsilon)(T_f+T_P).
\]
Consequently, an oracle bound counting only objective calls does not constitute an end-to-end efficiency guarantee when \(T_P\) is unavailable, grows superlinearly with problem representation size, or dominates \(T_f\). This is the expensive-projection boundary: projection-based complexity ceases to predict computational cost, motivating conditional-gradient, cutting-plane, penalty, or functional-constraint access models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration bounds based only on subgradient calls become computationally misleading when each exact projection is unavailable or substantially more expensive than the objective oracle.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration requires one exact projection and one objective-oracle call.
\(N(\varepsilon)\) iterations are required for the stated accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The end-to-end cost is at least \(N(\varepsilon)(T_f+T_P)\), so objective-oracle complexity alone is inadequate when projection dominates.

notation.meaning: Iteration count required for accuracy epsilon.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary cost accounting is coherent, but the claimed computational boundary and the listed alternative access models depend on a specified cost model and require an authoritative source.

children.title: Nonsmooth Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective structures that change method selection, averaging, or attainable guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: General Lipschitz Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard bounded-subgradient regime for nonsmooth convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. The general Lipschitz convex regime holds with constant \(L<\infty\) when
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\quad\text{for all }x,y\in C.
\]
If \(C\) is open, this is equivalent to \(\|g\|_*\leq L\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(g\in\partial f(x)\). On a closed constrained domain, uniformly bounded subgradients imply the displayed Lipschitz inequality, while the converse may require relative-interior or extension qualifications near the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex objective is in the general Lipschitz regime when its value changes at most linearly with distance; bounded subgradients provide the standard oracle characterization.
assumptions_latex: The norm and its dual norm are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(C\), with bounded-subgradient equivalence on open domains.

notation.meaning: Dual norm associated with the ambient norm.
Convex subdifferential of the objective at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Nonsmooth Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convexity of a constrained nonsmooth objective stated through its extended-valued subgradient inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Define \(F=f+\delta_C\). The constrained problem is in the strongly convex nonsmooth regime with modulus \(\mu>0\) when, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\), every \(g\in\partial F(x)\), and every \(y\in\operatorname{dom}F\),
\[
F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2.
\]
No differentiability is required. If \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in E}F(x)\), then \(x^*\) is unique and
\[
f(x)-f(x^*)\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-x^*\rVert^2
\quad\text{for every }x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended constrained objective lies above each of its subgradient affine models by a positive quadratic term. Any attained constrained minimizer is unique and satisfies quadratic growth.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\).
The displayed inequality holds for \(F=f+\delta_C\) with some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any attained minimizer \(x^*\) is unique and satisfies \(f(x)-f(x^*)\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert x-x^*\rVert^2\) for every feasible \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of the constrained extended objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Nonsmooth Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex objective split into a subgradient-oracle term and a term retained in a proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and consider
\[
\min_{x\in C}F(x),\qquad F(x)=f(x)+h(x),
\]
where \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, and convex. The problem is in the composite nonsmooth regime when \(f\) is accessed through values and subgradients while \(h\) is retained exactly through an available proximal or Bregman-proximal subproblem. Specifically, for a chosen differentiable strictly convex generator \(\omega\), an admissible base point \(x_k\), a subgradient \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), and a stepsize \(\eta_k>0\), the required access returns a minimizer of
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{\langle g_k,x\rangle+h(x)+\eta_k^{-1}D_{\omega}(x,x_k)\right\},
\]
whenever this minimizer set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective splits into a convex term handled through subgradients and a convex term retained exactly through an available proximal or Bregman-proximal subproblem.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) and \(h\) are proper, closed, and convex, and their domains meet \(C\).
\(\omega\) is differentiable and strictly convex wherever the displayed Bregman divergence is evaluated.
The displayed proximal minimizer set is nonempty for admissible queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f+h\) permits updates that linearize \(f\) while retaining \(h\) exactly in the selected proximal geometry.

notation.meaning: Convex term retained in the proximal subproblem.
Bregman divergence generated by the selected function omega.
Positive stepsize for the proximal subproblem.

children.title: Sharp Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth objective families organized by sharp growth near solution sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weak-sharp-minimum condition of order one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed set, let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), assume the optimal value \(f^*=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) is finite, and let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) be nonempty. The objective has global sharpness with constant \(\alpha>0\) when
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \alpha\,\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\quad\text{for every }x\in C.
\]
A local sharp regime replaces \(C\) by a specified neighborhood of \(X^*\). The exponent-one growth is essential: it distinguishes sharpness from quadratic growth and from general Hölderian growth conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective suboptimality grows at least linearly with distance to the solution set, globally or on a specified neighborhood for the local version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\) on the stated region.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponent-one sharpness condition is coherent and fits the leaf, but neither its weak-sharp-minimum terminology nor the stated local/global variants have a cited locator.

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective families admitting residual-based control of distance or suboptimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölderian distance-to-solution error bound expressed through objective residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed set, let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and suppose \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is nonempty with finite value \(f^*\). An objective-residual Hölder error bound holds on a set \(S\subseteq C\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\theta>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq \kappa\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)^{\theta}
\quad\text{for every }x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}f.
\]
The regime is global when \(S=C\) and local when \(S\) is a specified neighborhood or sublevel set. The common linear residual error bound corresponds to \(\theta=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to the solution set is bounded by a power of objective suboptimality on a stated global, local, or sublevel region.
assumptions_latex: The validity region \(S\subseteq C\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\kappa(f(x)-f^*)^{\theta}\) for every admissible \(x\in S\).

notation.meaning: Region on which the error bound holds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual error-bound formula is plausible, but the admissible Hölder exponent convention, residual choice, and local/global validity regions require alignment with an authoritative source.

children.title: Sharpness–Error-Bound Relations
children.top_down_role: Implications, equivalence regimes, and separation boundaries between the regularity notions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness–Error-Bound Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reciprocal equivalence between power growth and objective-residual error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\), let \(f^*\) be finite, and fix a validity region \(S\subseteq C\). For constants \(c>0\) and \(p>0\), the growth condition
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq c\,\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^p
\]
for every \(x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) is algebraically equivalent to the objective-residual error bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq c^{-1/p}\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)^{1/p}.
\]
Hence exponent-one sharpness is exactly the linear residual error bound with reciprocal constants: \(p=1\), \(\theta=1\), and \(\kappa=1/c\), provided both statements use the same region and solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-growth inequality and its objective-residual error bound are equivalent by inversion; linear sharpness corresponds exactly to an exponent-one error bound.
assumptions_latex: Both inequalities use the same validity region \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Power growth of order \(p\) is equivalent to a residual error bound with exponent \(1/p\) and constant \(c^{-1/p}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic equivalence is correct on a common region, but it has no citation. The terminal relation is a property/equivalence, not mathematical duality; a sourced resubmission should use content_kind property.

children.title: Dual Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth optimization viewed through dual objectives and multiplier representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave Lagrangian dual objective represented as an infimum of affine functions of explicitly typed multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) be linear with \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), and let \(c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m):X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) have convex components. For the problem
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x):Ax=b,\ c(x)\leq0\},
\]
the Lagrangian dual objective is
\[
d(y,\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}\left\{f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle+\langle\lambda,c(x)\rangle\right\},
\qquad (y,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}_+^m.
\]
As a pointwise infimum of affine functions of \((y,\lambda)\), \(d\) is concave and may be nonsmooth. If the inner infimum is finite and attained at \(x_{y,\lambda}\in X\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), then
\[
\bigl(Ax_{y,\lambda}-b,c(x_{y,\lambda})\bigr)\in\partial^+d(y,\lambda).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Lagrangian dual objective is a concave, potentially nonsmooth infimum of affine functions of the multipliers. A primal point attaining a finite inner infimum supplies a constraint-residual supergradient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex, and \(f\) and the components of \(c\) are convex on their stated domains.
The inner infimum is finite and attained when the supergradient formula is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is concave, and \(\bigl(Ax_{y,\lambda}-b,c(x_{y,\lambda})\bigr)\in\partial^+d(y,\lambda)\) whenever the inner infimum is finite and attained.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative multiplier for the inequality constraints.
Concave superdifferential of the dual objective.

children.title: Decomposable Objective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objectives structured into separately accessible components or blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposable Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additively separable objectives with coupling confined to an aggregating operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_i\) be nonempty convex sets and let \(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). A decomposable objective regime has product variable \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) and representation
\[
F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)+h\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i\right),
\]
where \(h\) is convex and the linear maps \(A_i\) encode all coupling. If \(h\) is dualized through its conjugate, then
\[
F(x)=\sup_y\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(f_i(x_i)+\langle A_i^*y,x_i\rangle\bigr)-h^*(y)\right\},
\]
so minimization over the blocks separates for each fixed dual variable whenever the required interchange and attainment conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is a sum of block-local terms plus one linearly aggregated coupling term; conjugate dualization makes the block minimizations separable.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) is nonempty and convex, and each \(f_i\) is proper and convex.
The conjugate representation is evaluated where it is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(y\), the dualized expression separates into independent functions of the blocks \(x_i\).

notation.meaning: Linear map from block i into the coupling space.
Fenchel conjugate of the coupling function.
Adjoint of the block coupling map.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separable representation is plausible, but no source supports the selected dual-decomposition version. The common coupling space and dual variable are also untyped, and fixed-dual block separability should be distinguished from any minimax interchange or attainment claim.

children.title: Dual Decomposition Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Problem structures where dualization exposes componentwise computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Decomposition Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable convex programs coupled by a single affine constraint and accessed through their Lagrangian dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,m\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(A_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^p\) be linear; also let \(b\in\mathbb R^p\). For the problem \(\inf\{\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\}\), define, for \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^p\), \(L(x,\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)+\langle\lambda,\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i-b\rangle\). Its dual interface decomposes as \[q(\lambda)=-\langle\lambda,b\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^m\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+\langle A_i^{\mathsf T}\lambda,x_i\rangle\bigr).\] If each infimum is finite and attained at \(x_i(\lambda)\), then \(r(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i(\lambda)-b\) is a supergradient of the concave function \(q\) at \(\lambda\), equivalently \(-r(\lambda)\in\partial(-q)(\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the coupling constraint separates dual evaluation into independent block problems; the aggregate constraint residual from block minimizers supplies a supergradient of the dual function.
assumptions_latex: \(p,m\in\mathbb N\), \(X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) is nonempty and convex, and \(f_i:X_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
\(A_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\).
At the queried \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^p\), every displayed block infimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is block-separable up to \(-\langle\lambda,b\rangle\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^mA_ix_i(\lambda)-b\) is a supergradient of \(q\) at \(\lambda\).

children.title: Classical Subgradient Algorithms
children.top_down_role: Canonical unconstrained and projection-based schemes.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical unconstrained subgradient iteration for minimizing a proper convex function in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), an initial point \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)_{k\ge0}\), and an iteration limit \(T\), repeat for \(k=0,\ldots,T-1\): choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\); if \(g_k=0\), stop and return \(x_k\); otherwise set \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k.\] If no zero subgradient is encountered, return either the best iterate \(x_{k_*}\), where \(k_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le k<T}f(x_k)\), or the weighted average \(\bar x_T=(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k)\), according to the declared output convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, select a subgradient and move in its negative direction; return a zero-subgradient point, the best iterate, or a declared weighted average.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex, and every queried point has a nonempty subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated iterates satisfy \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kg_k\) with \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\).

notation.meaning: chosen convex subgradient at the current iterate

source_refs.locator: 8 Primal and Dual Projected Subgradient Methods p. 195

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Primal and Dual Projected Subgradient Methods p. 195

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Projection Scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projected subgradient method with an exactly evaluated metric projection onto a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Given \(x_0\in C\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_k)\), and a limit \(T\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and compute \[x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_kg_k),\qquad P_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\frac12\lVert z-y\rVert_2^2.\] Stop early if \(0\in\partial f(x_k)+N_C(x_k)\); otherwise, after \(T\) iterations return the declared best iterate or weighted average. Exact projection means that the displayed minimization is solved to global optimality at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take a subgradient step and then compute the exact Euclidean nearest feasible point; stop at a constrained first-order stationary point or return the declared aggregate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x_0\in C\).
\(f\) is proper and convex with a subgradient available at each iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iterate obeys \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_kg_k)\in C\).

notation.meaning: exact Euclidean projection onto the feasible set
convex-analytic normal cone to the feasible set at x

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Projection Scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected subgradient iteration whose Euclidean projection subproblem is solved with a certified additive objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Given \(x_0\in C\), stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\), projection tolerances \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\), and limit \(T\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), set \(y_k=x_k-\alpha_kg_k\), and choose \(x_{k+1}\in C\) satisfying \[\frac12\lVert x_{k+1}-y_k\rVert_2^2\le \inf_{z\in C}\frac12\lVert z-y_k\rVert_2^2+\varepsilon_k.\] Stop if a declared constrained optimality test holds; otherwise return the declared best iterate or weighted average after \(T\) iterations. The case \(\varepsilon_k=0\) reduces to exact Euclidean projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After each subgradient step, return a feasible point whose squared-distance projection objective is within a prescribed additive tolerance of its optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(x_0\in C\).
\(f\) is proper and convex with \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(x_{k+1}\) is feasible and satisfies the displayed additive projection-error certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Additive projection-objective error is one particular inexact-projection convention and is not determined by the node title. An authoritative source is required to support this exact certificate and algorithmic variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Projection Scheme
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-metric projected subgradient method using uniformly positive-definite scaling matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Given \(x_0\in C\), stepsizes \(\alpha_k>0\), symmetric positive-definite matrices \(H_k\), and limit \(T\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and compute \[x_{k+1}=P_C^{H_k}(x_k-\alpha_kH_k^{-1}g_k),\qquad P_C^{H}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\frac12\lVert z-y\rVert_H^2.\] Require uniform spectral bounds \(mI\preceq H_k\preceq MI\) for constants \(0<m\le M<\infty\). Stop at a declared constrained optimality test; otherwise return the declared best iterate or weighted average after \(T\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precondition the subgradient by a positive-definite matrix and project exactly in the corresponding weighted norm, with scaling matrices uniformly bounded above and below.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is the exact \(H_k\)-metric projection of \(x_k-\alpha_kH_k^{-1}g_k\) onto \(C\).

notation.meaning: weighted norm defined by the square root of v-transpose-H-v
projection onto C in the H metric

children.title: Subgradient Stepsize Families
children.top_down_role: Policies separated by the horizon, scale, and target information they require.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Stepsize Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed positive stepsize assignment for all iterations of a subgradient method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constant stepsize policy chooses a scalar \(\alpha>0\) before iteration and imposes \[\alpha_k=\alpha\qquad\text{for every }k\ge0.\] For a normalized subgradient update \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k/\lVert g_k\rVert_2)\), the same definition applies to the step length \(\alpha_k\); for an unnormalized update \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\), it applies to the multiplier of \(g_k\). The selected convention must remain fixed throughout the run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose one positive step parameter and use it at every iteration, while explicitly fixing whether it multiplies a raw or normalized subgradient.
assumptions_latex: A raw-subgradient or normalized-subgradient update convention has been fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k=\alpha\) for all \(k\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Diminishing Stepsize Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robbins–Monro-type diminishing stepsizes for deterministic convex subgradient convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A square-summable but nonsummable diminishing stepsize policy is a deterministic sequence \((\alpha_k)_{k\ge0}\) satisfying \[\alpha_k>0,\qquad \alpha_k\to0,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty,\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2<\infty.\] A standard power-law instance is \(\alpha_k=a/(k+1)^p\) with \(a>0\) and \(1/2<p\le1\). This condition is attached to the multiplier of the raw subgradient in the projected or unprojected subgradient update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use positive steps that vanish, have infinite total length, and have finite squared total length; power laws with exponent above one-half and at most one qualify.
assumptions_latex: The stepsizes are deterministic positive scalars.
The update multiplies the raw subgradient by \(\alpha_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_k\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k\alpha_k^2<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Tuned Stepsize Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant stepsize tuned to a known iteration horizon for Lipschitz convex minimization over a bounded-distance domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and suppose \(\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2\le R\) and every selected subgradient satisfies \(\lVert g_k\rVert_2\le G\). For a known horizon \(T\ge1\), run projected subgradient descent with \[\alpha_k=\frac{R}{G\sqrt{T}}\qquad(0\le k<T)\] and return \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}x_k\). Then \[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)\le\frac{RG}{\sqrt{T}}.\] Thus \(T\ge(RG/\varepsilon)^2\) suffices for objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a known horizon, choose the constant step R divided by G times the square root of T; the averaged iterate has objective error at most RG divided by the square root of T.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and attains its minimum over nonempty closed convex \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)\le RG/\sqrt{T}\), so the iteration complexity is \(O(R^2G^2/\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on initial distance to an optimizer
uniform bound on selected subgradient norms

knowledge_statements.title: Known-Optimal-Value Policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak subgradient steps using the known attained optimal objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), assume the attained value \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is known, and start from \(x_0\in C\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(f(x_k)=f^*\), stop and return \(x_k\). If \(g_k\ne0\), choose a relaxation \(\gamma_k\in(0,2)\), set \[\alpha_k=
\gamma_k\frac{f(x_k)-f^*}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2},\qquad x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-
\alpha_kg_k),\] and continue until the declared iteration limit, then return the best objective iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the optimal value is known, scale the step by the current objective gap divided by the squared subgradient norm, optionally with relaxation below two.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and attains its known minimum value \(f^*\) over closed convex \(C\).
\(x_0\in C\), and a nonzero \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) is available whenever \(f(x_k)>f^*\).

\(\alpha_k=
\gamma_k(f(x_k)-f^*)/\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2\) and \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-
\alpha_kg_k)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Estimated-Target Policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyak-type steps formed with a supplied target value in place of the unknown optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), fix a target \(\tau\in\mathbb R\), and initialize \(x_0\in C\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). If \(f(x_k)\le	au\), stop and return \(x_k\). Otherwise, if \(g_k\ne0\), choose \(\gamma_kin(0,2)\) and set \[\alpha_k=
\gamma_k\frac{f(x_k)-	au}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2},\qquad x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-
\alpha_kg_k).\] Continue to the declared iteration limit and return the best objective iterate if the target has not been reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the unknown optimum in the Polyak formula by a fixed target; stop when the objective reaches that target, otherwise return the best iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on nonempty closed convex \(C\), and \(x_0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
While \(f(x_k)>	au\), the method uses \(\alpha_k=
\gamma_k(f(x_k)-	au)/\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular fixed-target variant, and the statement contains malformed TeX in \gamma_kin(0,2). The admissible relation of the target to the optimum and the intended guarantees also require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Target-Value Policy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-based Polyak policy that lowers its target after successful level attainment or unsuccessful phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose an initial level \(L_0<f(x_0)\), decrements \(\delta_j>0\), phase budgets \(B_j\in\mathbb N\), and relaxations \(\gamma_k\in(0,2)\). During phase \(j\), use the target \(\tau_j=L_j-
\delta_j\) and, while \(f(x_k)>	au_j\), update \[\alpha_k=
\gamma_k\frac{f(x_k)-	au_j}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2},\qquad x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-
\alpha_kg_k).\] If an iterate satisfies \(f(x_k)\le	au_j\), set \(L_{j+1}=f(x_k)\); if \(B_j\) phase iterations expire first, set \(L_{j+1}=L_j\). In either case, select a new positive decrement and begin the next phase. Return the incumbent with smallest objective value at termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run Polyak steps against a phase target below the incumbent level, then revise the level and decrement after reaching the target or exhausting the phase budget.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on nonempty closed convex \(C\), and nonzero subgradients are available above each target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Each phase uses target \(\tau_j=L_j-
\delta_j\) and updates the level according to target attainment before starting another phase.

notation.meaning: incumbent objective level at phase j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Adaptive level methods have materially different phase, decrement, budget, and restart rules. No source is supplied for this particular construction, so its exact algorithm cannot be validated.

children.title: Doubling Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies that expand guessed scales, budgets, or horizons across successive phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Doubling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic horizon-doubling wrapper for converting a horizon-tuned subgradient routine into an anytime procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A(H,z)\) be a base routine initialized at \(z\) and configured for exactly \(H\) oracle calls. Choose \(H_0\in\mathbb N\), set \(z_0=x_0\), and for epochs \(j=0,1,2,\ldots\) set \(H_j=2^jH_0\), run \(y_j=\mathcal A(H_j,z_j)\), record \(y_j\), and set \(z_{j+1}=y_j\). Stop when the cumulative oracle-call budget is exhausted and return the recorded point having the smallest observed objective value. If the final epoch has insufficient remaining budget, run its valid truncated form or return the best point from completed epochs, as fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a horizon-dependent base method in epochs whose lengths double, warm-start each epoch from the preceding output, and return the best recorded point.
assumptions_latex: The base routine \(\mathcal A(H,z)\) is defined for every integer horizon \(H\ge H_0\).
Objective values at recorded epoch outputs are available for selecting the incumbent.
The treatment of an incomplete final epoch is declared before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Epoch \(j\) has horizon \(H_j=2^jH_0\), and the returned point is the best recorded epoch output.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed warm-started horizon-doubling wrapper is plausible but is not uniquely determined by the title. Its restart state, output selection, and incomplete-epoch conventions require a supporting source.

children.title: Restart Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies that relaunch a subgradient schedule from a revised operating regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic epochwise restart wrapper for a projected subgradient method with geometrically enlarged scale estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), an initial point \(x^{(0)}\in C\), an initial scale \(R_0>0\), and an epoch budget rule \(T_j\), set \(R_j=2^jR_0\). During epoch \(j\), run a projected subgradient method from \(x^{(j)}\) for at most \(T_j\) iterations using the scale-dependent stepsize rule \(\alpha_{j,t}=\alpha_t(R_j)>0\). If the prescribed restart trigger occurs, terminate the epoch, choose its designated output \(\widehat x_j\in C\), and initialize the next epoch by \(x^{(j+1)}=\widehat x_j\). Otherwise return \(\widehat x_j\). After a finite global budget, return the designated output of the last completed epoch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run subgradient epochs under a current scale estimate, double that estimate when a trigger fires, and restart from the preceding epoch’s designated output.
assumptions_latex: Each epoch uses a well-defined projected subgradient update and a finite budget \(T_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{j+1}=2R_j\) at every triggered restart, and every epoch initialization and returned output belongs to \(C\).

notation.meaning: scale estimate used in epoch j

review_flags: Exact restart trigger and epoch-output conventions vary across parameter-free subgradient methods.
REQUEST_SOURCES: no supplied locator specifically documents the doubling-restart wrapper.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the Restart Policies leaf, but no cited source identifies this particular doubling wrapper, trigger behavior, epoch budget convention, or last-completed-epoch output rule. These choices vary materially across parameter-free subgradient methods.

children.title: Restart Trigger Regimes
children.top_down_role: Observable events or phase criteria used to initiate restarts.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Trigger Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable trigger predicates for epochwise scale-doubling subgradient policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let epoch \(j\) start at \(x^{(j)}\), use scale estimate \(R_j>0\), and generate iterates \(x_{j,0},x_{j,1},\ldots\) with observed subgradients \(g_{j,t}\). A restart-trigger regime is a sequence of predicates \(\tau_{j,t}\in\{0,1\}\), each measurable with respect to the history through time \(t\). The epoch stops at \(\sigma_j=\inf\{t\geq 0:\tau_{j,t}=1\}\). Typical admissible regimes include a fixed-budget trigger \(\tau_{j,t}=\mathbf 1\{t=T_j\}\), a radius trigger \(\tau_{j,t}=\mathbf 1\{\|x_{j,t}-x^{(j)}\|>R_j\}\), and an accumulated-scale trigger \(\tau_{j,t}=\mathbf 1\{\sum_{s=0}^{t}\alpha_{j,s}\|g_{j,s}\|>R_j\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restart time is the first history-measurable event indicating that an epoch budget, displacement bound, or accumulated subgradient scale has been exceeded.
assumptions_latex: The trigger uses only information observed by the end of the current iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_j\) is a stopping time for the epoch history and determines whether and when the scale is enlarged.

notation.meaning: first triggered iteration in epoch j

review_flags: The displayed regimes are generic formalizations rather than a uniquely identified named policy.
REQUEST_SOURCES: a source fixing the intended trigger family is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the Restart Trigger Regimes leaf, and the stopping-time formalization is coherent. However, no source supports the asserted collection of fixed-budget, radius, and accumulated-scale triggers as the intended family; the last two formulas are policy-specific rather than canonical consequences of the parent container.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Dependent Stepsize Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar cumulative-subgradient stepsizes for Euclidean projected subgradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimizing a convex function \(f\) over a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), choose \(x_1\in C\), \(D>0\), and \(\delta>0\). At iteration \(t\), obtain \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\), form \(S_t=\delta^2+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\|g_s\|^2\), set \(\alpha_t=D/\sqrt{S_t}\), and update \[x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\alpha_t g_t).\] After \(T\) iterations, return either a specified iterate or the weighted average \(\bar x_T=(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_t x_t)/(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_t)\). Thus each stepsize is determined by observed subgradient magnitudes rather than a preassigned Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale each projected subgradient step by the inverse square root of the cumulative observed squared subgradient norms.
assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and subdifferentiable at every generated iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_t>0\) is history-measurable and nonincreasing, and \(x_{t+1}\in C\) for every \(t\).

children.title: Structured Subgradient Variants
children.top_down_role: Classical variants created by stochastic, componentwise, dual, or functional-constraint information flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Projected Subgradient Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-unbiased stochastic subgradient iteration for constrained convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\). Choose \(x_1\in C\) and positive stepsizes \((\alpha_t)\). At iteration \(t\), sample \(\xi_t\), compute a stochastic subgradient \(G_t\), and update \[x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\alpha_tG_t).\] With \(\mathcal F_t\) denoting the information available before sampling \(\xi_t\), require \(\mathbb{E}[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]\in\partial f(x_t)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\|G_t\|^2\mid\mathcal F_t]<\infty\). After \(T\) oracle calls, return the prescribed last, best, or averaged iterate in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project each iterate after stepping along a conditionally unbiased stochastic subgradient of the expected convex objective.
assumptions_latex: The stochastic oracle is conditionally unbiased and has finite conditional second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\in C\) for all \(t\), and the conditional mean search direction belongs to \(\partial f(x_t)\).

notation.meaning: stochastic subgradient returned at iteration t

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Projected Subgradient Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclic or prescribed-order component subgradient updates for finite-sum convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x)\) on a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\). Choose \(x_1\in C\), positive stepsizes \((\alpha_t)\), and an index sequence \(i_t\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), such as \(i_t=1+((t-1)\bmod m)\). At iteration \(t\), select \(g_t\in\partial f_{i_t}(x_t)\) and update \[x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\alpha_tg_t).\] One cycle consists of \(m\) consecutive component updates. After the prescribed number of updates or cycles, return a specified feasible iterate or an average of feasible iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process one convex component at a time, taking a projected component-subgradient step according to a cyclic or otherwise prescribed index sequence.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper, convex, and subdifferentiable at generated points in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\in C\) for all \(t\), while each update requires a subgradient of only the selected component \(f_{i_t}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Functional-Constraint Subgradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Switching projected subgradient scheme for a convex objective subject to convex functional inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in C}f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex. Choose \(x_1\in C\), tolerances \(\varepsilon_t\geq0\), and stepsizes \(\alpha_t>0\). If \(\max_i f_i(x_t)\leq\varepsilon_t\), choose \(g_t\in\partial f_0(x_t)\); otherwise choose an index \(i_t\) with \(f_{i_t}(x_t)>\varepsilon_t\) and \(g_t\in\partial f_{i_t}(x_t)\). Set \[x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\alpha_tg_t).\] Return a designated approximately feasible iterate or an average of objective-update iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use an objective subgradient at approximately feasible points and a violated-constraint subgradient otherwise, projecting every update onto the simple set.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are proper convex functions subdifferentiable at generated iterates.
The violated constraint can be identified whenever the feasibility test fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iterate lies in \(C\), and each iteration targets either objective decrease or correction of a detected functional-constraint violation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Projected Subgradient Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected subgradient ascent on the concave Lagrange dual over nonnegative multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex program \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(h_i(x)\leq0\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,h(x)\rangle\) and \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\) on \(\mathbb{R}_+^m\). Choose \(\lambda_1\geq0\) and \(\alpha_t>0\). At iteration \(t\), choose \(x_t\in\arg\min_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda_t)\), set \(s_t=h(x_t)\in\partial^+q(\lambda_t)\), and update \[\lambda_{t+1}=P_{\mathbb{R}_+^m}(\lambda_t+\alpha_ts_t).\] After \(T\) iterations, return a designated dual iterate and, when required, a weighted average of the primal minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ascend the concave dual function using constraint residuals from Lagrangian minimizers, projecting multipliers onto the nonnegative orthant.
assumptions_latex: The Lagrangian infimum is attained at each generated multiplier.
The dual function is finite at generated multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_t\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(h(x_t)\in\partial^+q(\lambda_t)\) for every \(t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Subgradient Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous projected descent-ascent for a convex-concave saddle formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(Y\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). Choose \((x_1,y_1)\in X\times Y\) and \(\alpha_t>0\). At iteration \(t\), select \(g_t^x\in\partial_xL(x_t,y_t)\) and \(g_t^y\in\partial_y^+L(x_t,y_t)\), then update \[x_{t+1}=P_X(x_t-\alpha_tg_t^x),\qquad y_{t+1}=P_Y(y_t+\alpha_tg_t^y).\] After \(T\) iterations, return the weighted averages \(\bar x_T=(\sum_t\alpha_tx_t)/(\sum_t\alpha_t)\) and \(\bar y_T=(\sum_t\alpha_ty_t)/(\sum_t\alpha_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply projected subgradient descent to the primal variable and projected supergradient ascent to the dual variable, usually returning weighted averages.
assumptions_latex: \(L(\cdot,y)\) is proper convex on \(X\) and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is proper concave on \(Y\).
The displayed partial subgradients and supergradients exist at generated iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_t,y_t)\in X\times Y\) for every \(t\), and \((\bar x_T,\bar y_T)\in X\times Y\).

notation.meaning: subdifferential in the convex primal variable
superdifferential in the concave dual variable

knowledge_statements.title: Best-Iterate Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-selected output among finitely many feasible subgradient iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in C\) be feasible iterates for minimizing a real-valued function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). A best-iterate output is any \[\widehat x_T\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq t\leq T} f(x_t).\] Equivalently, choose an index \(t_T^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq t\leq T}f(x_t)\) using a fixed tie-breaking rule and set \(\widehat x_T=x_{t_T^*}\). Then \(f(\widehat x_T)=\min_{1\leq t\leq T}f(x_t)\) and \(\widehat x_T\in C\). This output policy requires evaluating or otherwise comparing the objective values of the candidate iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return a generated feasible iterate having the smallest observed objective value, with a fixed rule for resolving ties.
assumptions_latex: Every \(x_t\) lies in \(C\) and every \(f(x_t)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x_T\in C\) and \(f(\widehat x_T)=\min_{1\leq t\leq T}f(x_t)\).

assumptions_latex: \(T\geq 1\), the averaging domains are convex, and all averaged iterates belong to their respective domains.
The objective is convex; in the saddle extension, \(L\) is convex in its first variable and concave in its second variable.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\geq 1\), let \(C\) be convex, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in C\), and let weights \(w_t\geq 0\) satisfy \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t>0\). Define the ergodic output \(\bar x_T=W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_tx_t\). For every convex function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\), \[\bar x_T\in C,\qquad f(\bar x_T)\leq\frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_tf(x_t).\] More generally, let \(X\) and \(Y\) be convex, let \(x_t\in X\) and \(y_t\in Y\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\), define \(\bar x_T=W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_tx_t\) and \(\bar y_T=W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_ty_t\), and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second. Then, for every \((x,y)\in X\times Y\), \[L(\bar x_T,y)-L(x,\bar y_T)\leq\frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t\bigl(L(x_t,y)-L(x,y_t)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted average of feasible iterates remains feasible, and convexity transfers averaged objective values to an objective bound at the average. For convex-concave saddle functions, explicitly defined primal and dual weighted averages satisfy the analogous averaged gap bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\geq1\), let \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\) belong to a convex set \(C\), and let \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\geq0\) with \(W_t=\sum_{s=1}^{t}w_s\) and \(W_T>0\). The weighted-average output is \[\bar x_T=\frac{1}{W_T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_tx_t.\] It is a convex combination of the generated iterates and hence belongs to \(C\). In projected subgradient methods, the stepsize-weighted choice \(w_t=\alpha_t\) yields \(\bar x_T=(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_tx_t)/(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_t)\) whenever \(\alpha_t>0\). For every \(t\geq2\) such that \(W_{t-1}>0\), the output can be updated online by \[\bar x_t=\frac{W_{t-1}\bar x_{t-1}+w_tx_t}{W_t}.\] If initial weights vanish, initialize the recursion at the first index \(r\) with \(w_r>0\) by setting \(\bar x_r=x_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return a convex combination of generated iterates, commonly using stepsizes as weights. The average has an online recursion once the preceding cumulative weight is positive; if initial weights vanish, initialize it at the first positive-weight iterate.

knowledge_statements.title: Output Weighting Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible weight sequences and standard regimes for finite ergodic outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For iterates \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\), an admissible output-weighting regime specifies history-measurable weights \(w_t\geq0\) such that \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t>0\), and returns \(\bar x_T=W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_tx_t\). Standard regimes include uniform weighting \(w_t=1\), stepsize weighting \(w_t=\alpha_t\), polynomial weighting \(w_t=t^p\) for \(p\geq0\), and terminal-window weighting \(w_t=\mathbf 1\{t\geq T-k+1\}\) for \(1\leq k\leq T\). If the iterates lie in a convex feasible set, every such regime produces a feasible output; convergence rates depend on matching the weights to the underlying per-iteration inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose nonnegative weights with positive total mass; common choices are uniform, stepsize, polynomial, or terminal-window weights.
assumptions_latex: The weights are determined without using future oracle information, except when a fixed terminal horizon defines a window.
At least one weight is positive.
All averaged iterates lie in a common convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed regime defines a convex-combination output \(\bar x_T\) in the same feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Suffix-Averaged Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-size-weighted averaging over a terminal suffix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_0,\ldots,x_T\in C\), let \(m\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), and let weights \(w_t\ge 0\) satisfy \(\sum_{t=m}^{T}w_t>0\). The suffix-averaged output beginning at \(m\) is \[\widehat{x}_{T,m}:=\frac{\sum_{t=m}^{T}w_t x_t}{\sum_{t=m}^{T}w_t}.\] In subgradient methods one commonly takes \(w_t=\alpha_t\), the step size used at iteration \(t\). Because the coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one after normalization, convexity of \(C\) implies \(\widehat{x}_{T,m}\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Report a normalized weighted average of all iterates from a chosen suffix start m through the terminal index T.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and \(x_t\in C\) for \(m\le t\le T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{x}_{T,m}\in C\) and \(\widehat{x}_{T,m}=\bigl(\sum_{t=m}^{T}w_t x_t\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{t=m}^{T}w_t\bigr)\).

children.title: Tail-Averaged Output
children.top_down_role: Terminal-window averages organized by tail length or tail proportion.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Averaged Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform averaging over the last prescribed number of iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0,\ldots,x_T\in C\) and an integer tail length \(q\in\{1,\ldots,T+1\}\), define the tail index set \(I_{T,q}:=\{T-q+1,\ldots,T\}\). The tail-averaged output is \[\bar{x}^{\mathrm{tail}}_{T,q}:=\frac{1}{q}\sum_{t=T-q+1}^{T}x_t.\] Thus \(q=1\) recovers the last iterate, whereas \(q=T+1\) averages the entire trajectory. If \(C\) is convex and every retained iterate lies in \(C\), then \(\bar{x}^{\mathrm{tail}}_{T,q}\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Report the uniform average of the final q iterates; q=1 gives the last iterate and q=T+1 gives the full average.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and \(x_t\in C\) for \(t\in I_{T,q}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar{x}^{\mathrm{tail}}_{T,q}=q^{-1}\sum_{t=T-q+1}^{T}x_t\in C\).

children.title: Terminal Window Selection
children.top_down_role: Choices of starting index, window length, and horizon dependence for terminal averaging.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal Window Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility conditions for horizon-dependent terminal windows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every horizon \(T\ge 1\), choose a start index \(m_T\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\) and define the terminal window \(I_T:=\{m_T,m_T+1,\ldots,T\}\), with length \(q_T:=T-m_T+1\). A terminal-window rule is asymptotically expanding and genuinely terminal when \[q_T\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad \frac{q_T}{T+1}\longrightarrow\rho\quad\text{for some }\rho\in[0,1].\] The case \(\rho>0\) retains a fixed asymptotic fraction of the trajectory; \(\rho=0\) permits a vanishing fraction while still requiring infinitely many retained iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a contiguous final window whose length diverges; its retained fraction may converge to a positive constant or vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_T=\{m_T,\ldots,T\}\), \(q_T\to\infty\), and \(q_T/(T+1)\to\rho\in[0,1]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for treating divergence of the window length together with convergence of its retained fraction as the defining admissibility condition. This is a particular asymptotic convention rather than a source-independent consequence, so its exact formulation requires support.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Distance Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convexity relative to the norm used by mirror descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space equipped with norm \(\|\cdot\|\). A differentiable convex function \(h\) on an open convex set containing \(C\) is a \(\sigma\)-strongly convex distance-generating function on \(C\), where \(\sigma>0\), if for all \(x,y\in C\), \[h(x)\ge h(y)+\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|x-y\|^2.\] Equivalently, its Bregman divergence satisfies \(D_h(x,y)\ge(\sigma/2)\|x-y\|^2\) on \(C\times C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance generator is sigma-strongly convex when its linearization error dominates sigma/2 times the squared ambient norm distance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set containing \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,y)\ge \frac{\sigma}{2}\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Legendre Distance Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Legendre generators in the convex-analytic sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with \(U:=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\ne\varnothing\). The function \(h\) is a Legendre distance generator when it is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex: \(h\) is differentiable on \(U\), \(\|\nabla h(x_k)\|_*\to\infty\) whenever \(x_k\in U\) approaches a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}h\), and \(h\) is strictly convex on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h\). Its Bregman divergence is evaluated with second argument in \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre generator is a closed proper convex function that is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex on its effective domain.

children.title: Separable Distance Generators

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Distance Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise additive distance generators on product domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_n\) and write \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). A distance generator \(h:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is separable when there exist proper convex functions \(h_i:C_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_i(x_i).\] At points where every \(h_i\) is differentiable, the generated divergence decomposes as \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{h_i}(x_i,y_i).\] Consequently, a Bregman proximal subproblem also separates coordinatewise whenever its feasible set and remaining objective term have the same product-additive structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable generator is a sum of coordinate functions; its Bregman divergence is the sum of their coordinatewise divergences.
assumptions_latex: \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_n\) is a product of convex sets.
\(h_i\) is proper and convex on \(C_i\) for every \(i\).
Each \(h_i\) is differentiable at the divergence base point.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Distance Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive generators aligned with a prescribed block decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=X_1\times\cdots\times X_B\), let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_B\), and write \(x=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(B)})\). A block distance generator has the form \[h(x)=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\lambda_b h_b\bigl(x^{(b)}\bigr),\qquad \lambda_b>0,\] where each \(h_b\) is a distance generator on \(C_b\). Wherever the block gradients exist, \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\lambda_b D_{h_b}\bigl(x^{(b)},y^{(b)}\bigr).\] The weights permit different geometric scaling across blocks while preserving additive Bregman structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block generator is a positively weighted sum of blockwise generators, yielding the same weighted sum of block Bregman divergences.
assumptions_latex: Each \(h_b\) is differentiable at the divergence base point.
