knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Nonsmooth Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle upper complexity for strongly convex functions with bounded subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be closed and convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be \(\mu\)-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm. Assume \(f\) attains its minimum and the subgradients selected by projected subgradient descent satisfy \(\|g_t\|\le G\). With steps \(\eta_t=2/[\mu(t+1)]\) and linearly weighted output
\[\widetilde x_T=\frac{2}{T(T+1)}\sum_{t=1}^T t x_t,\]
one has
\[f(\widetilde x_T)-f^*\le\frac{2G^2}{\mu(T+1)}.\]
Consequently, \(O(G^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\) first-order oracle calls suffice for objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity improves nonsmooth first-order upper complexity from inverse-square to inverse-linear dependence on objective accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=O(G^2/(\mu\varepsilon))\) first-order oracle calls suffice

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth First-Order Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent deterministic local-oracle lower bound for Lipschitz convex minimization on a Euclidean ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\ge 1\), \(d\ge T+1\), and let \(B_R=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\|x\|_2\le R\}\). For every deterministic method whose query \(x_t\) depends only on preceding local first-order oracle responses \((f(x_i),g_i)\), there exists a convex \(G\)-Lipschitz function \(f:B_R\to\mathbb R\) and valid subgradients \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) such that its output \(\widehat x_T\in B_R\) satisfies \[f(\widehat x_T)-\min_{x\in B_R}f(x)\ge c\,\frac{GR}{\sqrt{T}},\] where \(c>0\) is a universal constant. Consequently, guaranteeing error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega((GR/\varepsilon)^2)\) oracle calls while the dimension supports the resisting-oracle construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic local first-order method can require order (GR/ε)² oracle calls for Lipschitz convex minimization, provided the dimension is at least proportional to the call budget.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns only a function value and one valid subgradient at each query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\widehat x_T)-f^*\ge cGR/\sqrt{T}\), hence \(T=\Omega((GR/\varepsilon)^2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimension-dependent resisting-oracle theorem is plausible, but no citation supports the precise oracle model, dimension condition, or universal-constant lower bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Complexity Refinements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains the dimension restriction in standard nonsmooth resisting-oracle lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard resisting-oracle construction for deterministic nonsmooth convex minimization in \(\mathbb R^d\), each of the first \(T\) oracle calls may require a new mutually orthogonal direction. Thus the usual lower bound \(cGR/\sqrt{T}\) is directly obtained only when \(T\le d-1\). For fixed \(d\), that construction cannot justify the same asymptotic lower bound for arbitrarily large \(T\): after at most \(d\) independent directions, the information-hiding argument is exhausted. Therefore any complexity assertion beyond this range must explicitly incorporate dimension or use a different oracle model or lower-bound construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical resisting-oracle lower bound uses one new direction per query and therefore applies directly only while the query count is below the ambient dimension.
assumptions_latex: The problem class consists of convex \(G\)-Lipschitz objectives on a radius-\(R\) Euclidean ball.
The lower-bound argument uses mutually orthogonal hidden directions in \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction supports \(f(\widehat x_T)-f^*\ge cGR/\sqrt{T}\) only in its dimension-valid regime \(T\\le d-1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative locator is required for the claimed limit of the resisting-oracle construction. The conclusion also contains a doubled backslash before the dimension inequality, so the intended \(T\le d-1\) is not validly encoded.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mirror-descent bound expressed through dual-norm subgradients and Bregman diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex, let \(h:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex with respect to a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and let \(D_h\) be its Bregman divergence. Suppose \(f\) is convex and \(\|g_t\|_*\le G\) for \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). Mirror descent with constant step \(\eta>0\) and weighted average \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T x_t\) satisfies \[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)\le \frac{D_h(x^*,x_1)}{\eta T}+\frac{\eta G^2}{2}.\] If \(D_h(x^*,x_1)\le D\), choosing \(\eta=\sqrt{2D/(G^2T)}\) yields \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le G\sqrt{2D/T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-descent complexity depends on the chosen norm’s dual subgradient bound and the prox geometry’s Bregman radius, giving error at most G√(2D/T).
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\).
\(f\) is convex and every selected subgradient satisfies \(\|g_t\|_*\le G\).
A minimizer \(x^*\in C\) exists and \(D_h(x^*,x_1)\le D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le G\sqrt{2D/T}\) for the stated constant step size.

notation.meaning: upper bound on initial Bregman distance to a minimizer

children.top_down_role: Guarantees not captured by best-value or ergodic complexity alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Subgradient Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic last-iterate convergence for projected subgradient descent with square-summable diminishing steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let the convex function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) attain its minimum. Consider \(x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\eta_t g_t)\), where \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\), \(\|g_t\|_2\le G\), \(\eta_t>0\), \(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta_t=\infty\), and \(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta_t^2<\infty\). Then the unaveraged iterates approach the solution set and their objective values converge: \[\operatorname{dist}(x_t,X^*)\to0,\qquad f(x_t)\to f^*.\] In particular, the guarantee concerns the actual last iterate rather than a best-so-far or ergodic output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With bounded subgradients and square-summable but nonsummable steps, projected subgradient descent’s actual iterates approach the solution set and their objective values approach optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
\(f\) is convex and the selected subgradients are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_t,X^*)\to0\) and \(f(x_t)\to f^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Mirror-Descent Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic last-iterate convergence under coercive Bregman geometry and diminishing steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) be closed and convex, let \(f\) be convex with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\), and let \(h\) be differentiable and strongly convex on \(C\). Define \[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\eta_t\langle g_t,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_t)\},\qquad g_t\in\partial f(x_t).\] If the selected dual-norm subgradients are bounded, \(\sum_t\eta_t=\infty\), \(\sum_t\eta_t^2<\infty\), and the relevant Bregman sublevel sets are compact, then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_t,X^*)\to0\) and \(f(x_t)\to f^*\). Thus the unaveraged final iterate is asymptotically optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under bounded subgradients, suitable Bregman compactness, and square-summable but nonsummable steps, mirror descent’s actual iterates approach the minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and strongly convex on \(C\), with compact relevant Bregman sublevel sets.
\(f\) is convex, \(X^*\ne\varnothing\), and \(\|g_t\|_*\) is uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_t,X^*)\to0\) and \(f(x_t)\to f^*\).

notation.meaning: minimizer set of f over C

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate-Sequence Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-sequence convergence of projected subgradient iterates in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(X^*\ne\varnothing\). For \(x_{t+1}=P_C(x_t-\eta_tg_t)\), assume \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\), \(\sup_t\|g_t\|_2<\infty\), \(\sum_t\eta_t=\infty\), and \(\sum_t\eta_t^2<\infty\). Then there exists \(x^\infty\in X^*\) such that \[x_t\to x^\infty.\] Hence the complete iterate sequence, not merely a subsequence or its objective values, converges to a single minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, projected subgradient iterates with bounded subgradients and standard diminishing steps converge as a full sequence to one minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on nonempty closed convex \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\), and \(X^*\ne\varnothing\).
The selected subgradients are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x^\infty\in X^*\) for which \(x_t\to x^\infty\).

notation.meaning: set of minimizers of f over C

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Value Quality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap certificate relative to a supplied valid target lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\), and suppose a target value \(\tau\) is known to satisfy \(\tau\le f^*\). For any feasible candidate \(\widehat x\in C\), define \(\Delta_\tau(\widehat x)=f(\widehat x)-\tau\). Then \[0\le f(\widehat x)-f^*\le \Delta_\tau(\widehat x).\] Consequently, the directly checkable conditions \(\widehat x\in C\) and \(f(\widehat x)\le\tau+\varepsilon\) certify \(\varepsilon\)-suboptimality. If \(\tau=f^*\), the certificate equals the exact objective gap; without the validity condition \(\tau\le f^*\), it is not a sound upper certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point within ε of a certified lower target τ is ε-optimal; the certificate is valid only when τ does not exceed the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat x\in C\) and \(f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\widehat x)-f^*\le f(\widehat x)-\tau\), so \(f(\widehat x)\le\tau+\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Best-Value Quality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-observed feasible objective value paired with any certified global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_T\in C\) be feasible evaluated points, define \(f_T^{\mathrm{best}}=\min_{1\le t\le T}f(x_t)\), and let \(L_T\le f^*=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) be any certified lower bound. If \(t_T\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le t\le T}f(x_t)\), then \[0\le f(x_{t_T})-f^*\le f_T^{\mathrm{best}}-L_T.\] Thus \(f_T^{\mathrm{best}}-L_T\le\varepsilon\) is a verifiable additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate for the stored best iterate. The certificate does not by itself certify the last iterate unless it attains the best recorded value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best evaluated feasible point is ε-optimal whenever its value differs by at most ε from a certified global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_{t_T})-f^*\le f_T^{\mathrm{best}}-L_T\).

notation.meaning: certified lower bound on the optimum

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Based Lower Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound obtained by minimizing an aggregate of subgradient affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex, let \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\), and let weights \(\lambda_t\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{t=1}^T\lambda_t=1\). Define the aggregate affine model \[m_T(x)=\sum_{t=1}^T\lambda_t\bigl(f(x_t)+\langle g_t,x-x_t\rangle\bigr),\qquad L_T=\inf_{x\in C}m_T(x).\] The subgradient inequality gives \(m_T(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\); hence \(L_T\le f^*\). If \(L_T\) is finite and its model minimization is solved or rigorously bounded below, then \(f(\widehat x)-L_T\) is a verifiable upper bound on the objective gap of every feasible \(\widehat x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex combination of subgradient affine minorants remains below the objective; minimizing it over the feasible set produces a certified lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The value \(L_T\) is finite and is computed or rigorously bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_T\le f^*\) and \(f(\widehat x)-f^*\le f(\widehat x)-L_T\) for every \(\widehat x\in C\).

children.title: Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates and recovery routes associated with explicit or functional constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility and distance certificate supplied by Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For any \(y\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(p=P_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\|x-y\|_2\). Then \(p\in C\), \(\|y-p\|_2=\operatorname{dist}(y,C)\), and \[\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\le0\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Thus \(p\) is an exactly feasible recovery of \(y\); the residual \(r=y-p\), together with the variational inequality, certifies both the projection and the exact magnitude of infeasibility. In particular, \(\|r\|_2\le\varepsilon\) certifies that \(y\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting onto a closed convex set produces an exactly feasible point, while the projection residual certifies the original point’s exact distance from feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(p\) is the exact Euclidean projection of \(y\) onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in C\), \(\|y-p\|_2=\operatorname{dist}(y,C)\), and \(\langle y-p,x-p\rangle\le0\) for all \(x\in C\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from y to C

knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Feasibility Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility recovery for convex constraints by averaging approximately feasible iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex, let \(x_t\in C\), and let \(h_j:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex constraint functions for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). For weights \(\lambda_t\ge0\) with \(\sum_{t=1}^T\lambda_t=1\), define \(\bar x_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\lambda_tx_t\). Convexity yields \[h_j(\bar x_T)\le\sum_{t=1}^T\lambda_th_j(x_t)\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).\] Therefore, bounds \(\sum_t\lambda_th_j(x_t)\le\varepsilon_j\) certify \(h_j(\bar x_T)\le\varepsilon_j\). In particular, nonpositive averaged violations recover an exactly feasible ergodic point, while uniformly bounded averaged violations recover an approximately feasible one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex constraints, the violation at a weighted average is no greater than the weighted average of violations, yielding an ergodic feasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: Each functional constraint \(h_j\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_j(\bar x_T)\le\sum_t\lambda_th_j(x_t)\), so averaged violation bounds certify feasibility of \(\bar x_T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Functional-Constraint Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar certificate for exact or approximate satisfaction of finitely many inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a set, let \(m\in\mathbb N\), and let \(h_j:C\to\mathbb R\) be evaluable for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Define the feasible region \(F=\{x\in C:h_j(x)\le0\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m\}\) and \[v(x)=\max_{1\le j\le m}[h_j(x)]_+,\qquad [a]_+=\max\{a,0\}.\] Then \(v(x)\ge0\) and \(v(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in F\). More generally, for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\), \[v(x)\le\varepsilon\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_j(x)\le\varepsilon\text{ for every }j=1,\ldots,m.\] This certificate measures constraint-value violation; without an error bound it need not bound the metric distance \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum positive constraint value is zero exactly at feasible points and, for any nonnegative ε, is at most ε exactly when every inequality is violated by no more than ε.
assumptions_latex: Every constraint value \(h_j(x)\) can be evaluated or rigorously bounded above.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=0\iff x\in F\), and for \(\varepsilon\ge0\), \(v(x)\le\varepsilon\iff h_j(x)\le\varepsilon\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Value Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certificates for convex inequality-constrained minimization via Lagrangian dual values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper convex functions, and define \(p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in X,\ f_i(x)\leq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), set \(L(x,\lambda)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)\) and \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\). A pair \((\lambda,\ell)\), with \(\ell\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\ell\leq q(\lambda)\) established by an exact evaluation or a rigorous lower bound, is a dual-value certificate. Weak duality gives \(\ell\leq q(\lambda)\leq p^*\); hence \(\ell\) is a valid lower bound on the primal optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative multiplier together with an exact or rigorously certified lower bound on its Lagrangian dual value provides a valid lower bound on the constrained primal optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and \(f_0,\ldots,f_m\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\leq q(\lambda)\leq p^*\).

notation.meaning: certified lower bound on the dual value

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Approximation Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori certification of approximate dual multipliers under strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex program and dual function \(q\) of the preceding record, assume strong duality, so \(d^*=p^*\), where \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\geq0}q(\lambda)\). Let \(\widehat{x}\) be primal feasible and \(\widehat{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\). If a certified dual lower bound \(\ell\leq q(\widehat{\lambda})\) satisfies \(f_0(\widehat{x})-\ell\leq\varepsilon\), then \(d^*-q(\widehat{\lambda})\leq\varepsilon\). Thus \((\widehat{x},\widehat{\lambda},\ell)\) certifies that \(\widehat{\lambda}\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal multiplier in dual objective value; it does not, without additional curvature, certify distance to the set of optimal multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal point and a small certified primal–dual value gap prove that the proposed multiplier is nearly optimal in dual value, not necessarily in norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A computable optimality certificate formed from primal and dual feasible values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a convex primal problem with optimal value \(p^*\) and a weakly dual dual problem with value function \(q\). For any primal-feasible \(\widehat{x}\) and dual-feasible \(\widehat{\lambda}\), define the primal–dual gap \(G(\widehat{x},\widehat{\lambda})=f_0(\widehat{x})-q(\widehat{\lambda})\). Weak duality implies \(G(\widehat{x},\widehat{\lambda})\geq0\). If \(G(\widehat{x},\widehat{\lambda})\leq\varepsilon\), then \(0\leq f_0(\widehat{x})-p^*\leq\varepsilon\) and \(0\leq p^*-q(\widehat{\lambda})\leq\varepsilon\). The same conclusions remain valid when \(q(\widehat{\lambda})\) is replaced by a certified lower bound \(\ell\leq q(\widehat{\lambda})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal value minus a feasible dual lower bound simultaneously certifies primal suboptimality and dual-value suboptimality.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat{x}\) is primal feasible and \(\widehat{\lambda}\) is dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(\widehat{x},\widehat{\lambda})\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow f_0(\widehat{x})-p^*\leq\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ p^*-q(\widehat{\lambda})\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Primal Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted recovery of a primal candidate from dual-method Lagrangian minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given dual iterates \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_T\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), positive weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\), and associated responses \(x_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda_t)\), set \(W_T=\sum_{t=1}^T w_t\) and output \(\bar{x}_T=W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w_t x_t\). If \(X\) is convex, then \(\bar{x}_T\in X\). For every convex function \(h:X\to\mathbb{R}\), Jensen's inequality gives \(h(\bar{x}_T)\leq W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w_t h(x_t)\); applying this to the objective and constraint functions converts weighted aggregate bounds into primal objective and feasibility bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average the Lagrangian minimizers using positive algorithmic weights; convexity transfers aggregate objective and constraint estimates to the recovered primal point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and all functions to be averaged are convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar{x}_T\in X\quad\text{and}\quad h(\bar{x}_T)\leq W_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T w_t h(x_t)\).

children.title: Stopping Policy Families
children.top_down_role: Stopping routes based on budgets, targets, or available certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Budget Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping after a predetermined number of first-order oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer budget \(T\geq1\) before execution. Starting from \(x_1\in X\), perform exactly one prescribed first-order oracle call and one method update at each iteration \(t=1,\ldots,T\), recording any weights required by the method. Stop immediately after the \(T\)-th oracle call and return the method's designated output, such as the last iterate \(x_{T+1}\), a best feasible iterate, or the weighted average \(\bar{x}_T\). The stopping decision depends only on the consumed budget and therefore makes no claim that a target accuracy has been observed; any quality guarantee must follow from an a priori bound evaluated at \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run exactly the prescribed number of oracle calls, then return the method-defined iterate or average; accuracy follows only from an a priori iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: Each counted iteration uses exactly one designated first-order oracle call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{oracle}}=T\), after which the designated output is returned.

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Value Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping when an admissible iterate reaches a prescribed objective target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization of \(f\) over a feasible set \(C\), choose a target value \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\). Given iterates \(x_t\), define \(T_\tau=\inf\{t\geq1:x_t\in C,\ f(x_t)\leq\tau\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Evaluate feasibility and the objective after each completed update; stop at \(T_\tau\) and return \(x_{T_\tau}\) when this index is finite. If \(\varepsilon\geq0\) and \(\tau=p^*+\varepsilon\), where \(p^*=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\), then the returned point satisfies \(0\leq f(x_{T_\tau})-p^*\leq\varepsilon\). If \(\tau<p^*\), the stopping condition is unattainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop at the first feasible iterate whose objective does not exceed the target. A target equal to the optimal value plus a nonnegative tolerance yields an objective error no larger than that tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility and \(f(x_t)\) can be evaluated at each tested iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\tau<\infty\Rightarrow x_{T_\tau}\in C\ \text{and}\ f(x_{T_\tau})\leq\tau\).

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Based Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stopping at the first iterate carrying a verifiable accuracy certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(t\), construct a candidate output \(z_t\) and a computable certificate value \(C_t\geq0\) satisfying the soundness implication \(C_t\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow \mathcal{E}(z_t)\leq\varepsilon\), where \(\mathcal{E}\) is the specified solution-error measure. Define \(T_\varepsilon=\inf\{t\geq1:C_t\leq\varepsilon\}\). Stop and return \(z_{T_\varepsilon}\) when this index is finite. For primal–dual iterates, one admissible choice is \(C_t=f_0(x_t)-q(\lambda_t)\), provided primal and dual feasibility and the dual value are certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop at the first iterate whose sound, computable certificate is below tolerance; a feasible primal–dual gap is a standard certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\varepsilon<\infty\Rightarrow \mathcal{E}(z_{T_\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon\).

children.title: Maximum Oracle Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces for objectives represented through attained maxima.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact active-index oracle for an attained pointwise maximum of convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{u\in U}\phi(x,u)\), where \(x\mapsto\phi(x,u)\) is convex for every \(u\), and assume the maximum is attained at every queried \(x\). A maximum oracle queried at \(x\) returns an active index \(u_x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in U}\phi(x,u)\), the value \(f(x)=\phi(x,u_x)\), and a vector \(g_x\in\partial_x\phi(x,u_x)\). Then \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\), so the returned pair satisfies \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\) for every point \(y\) in the common domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an attained pointwise maximum, return an active maximizer, its value, and a component subgradient; that subgradient is valid for the maximum function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in U}\phi(x,u),\ g_x\in\partial_x\phi(x,u_x)\Rightarrow g_x\in\partial f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-component subgradient interface is mathematically standard and fits the maximum-oracle leaf, but no source or inspectable locator supports the pointwise-maximum subgradient claim.

children.title: Supremum Oracle Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Oracle interfaces for objectives represented through possibly unattained suprema.

knowledge_statements.title: Supremum Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inexact subgradient oracle for a possibly unattained pointwise supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\sup_{u\in U}\phi(x,u)<+\infty\), with \(x\mapsto\phi(x,u)\) convex. Given a query \((x,\eta)\) with \(\eta>0\), a supremum oracle returns \(u_{x,\eta}\in U\) satisfying \(\phi(x,u_{x,\eta})\geq f(x)-\eta\), together with \(g_{x,\eta}\in\partial_x\phi(x,u_{x,\eta})\). For every \(y\) in the common domain, \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g_{x,\eta},y-x\rangle-\eta\). Thus the returned vector is an \(\eta\)-subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\), even when the supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return a nearly maximizing index and its component subgradient; the result is an inexact subgradient with additive error equal to the maximization tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\sup_{u\in U}\phi(x,u)\) is finite at the query.
An \(\eta\)-maximizing index can be produced for each \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g_{x,\eta},y-x\rangle-\eta\quad\text{for all }y\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The approximate-maximizer calculation correctly yields an eta-subgradient and distinguishes a supremum oracle from an attained maximum oracle, but the record has no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Attainment Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of attainment, nonattainment, finite indexing, or infinite indexing.

knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of exact maximum-oracle semantics when a finite supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=(0,1)\), \(x>0\), and \(\phi(x,u)=ux\). Then \(f(x)=\sup_{u\in U}ux=x\), but \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in U}ux=\varnothing\). Consequently, an interface required to return an exact maximizer cannot answer this query, although the supremum value is finite and \(f\) is smooth. For every \(\eta>0\), choosing \(u\in U\) with \(u\geq1-\eta/x\) yields \(ux\geq f(x)-\eta\). Thus replacing compactness or another attainment condition by mere finiteness necessitates an approximate supremum oracle rather than an exact maximum oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite supremum over an open index set need not have a maximizer, so exact maximum oracles fail while arbitrarily accurate supremum oracles remain possible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{u\in U}\phi(x,u)=x\quad\text{but}\quad\operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in U}\phi(x,u)=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and its failure-boundary classification are correct and self-contained, but the evidence contract still requires a source, locator, or explicit standard-field rationale.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leading-eigenpair oracle for subgradients of maximum-eigenvalue composites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\), where \(A_i\) are real symmetric matrices, and define \(f(x)=\lambda_{\max}(A(x))\). A spectral oracle queried at \(x\) returns \(f(x)\) and a unit eigenvector \(v\) satisfying \(A(x)v=f(x)v\). It then returns \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with components \(g_i=v^{\mathsf T}A_i v\). The matrix \(vv^{\mathsf T}\) is a subgradient of \(\lambda_{\max}\) at \(A(x)\), and the chain rule yields \(g\in\partial f(x)\). With a multiple leading eigenvalue, any unit vector in its eigenspace gives a valid subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A leading eigenvalue and unit leading eigenvector yield a subgradient of an affine maximum-eigenvalue function through quadratic forms with the coefficient matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(x)v=\lambda_{\max}(A(x))v,\ \lVert v\rVert_2=1\Rightarrow (v^{\mathsf T}A_i v)_{i=1}^n\in\partial f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leading-eigenvector formula is mathematically standard and the algorithm role fits the spectral-oracle leaf, but no authoritative spectral-subdifferential locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Oracle Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient evaluation for a marginal value function through an attained inner minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\), where \(Y\) is convex and \(F\) is jointly convex. At a query \(x\), suppose the infimum is attained at \(y_x\) and an inner oracle returns \(y_x\), \(V(x)=F(x,y_x)\), and a joint subgradient \((g_x,0)\in\partial F(x,y_x)\). A value-function oracle returns \((V(x),g_x)\). The joint subgradient inequality then gives \(V(z)\geq V(x)+\langle g_x,z-x\rangle\) for every \(z\) in the domain of \(V\); hence \(g_x\in\partial V(x)\). The zero component is an explicit inner optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained inner minimizer and a joint subgradient with zero inner component provide both the value and a valid subgradient of the marginal function.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is convex and \(F\) is jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_x\in\partial V(x)\).

children.title: Projection-Bregman Subproblem Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Computational routes for Euclidean projection, mirror projection, and generalized prox subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Form Projection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean mirror steps whose feasible-set projection has an explicit coordinate or linear-algebra formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex; let \(x,g\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\eta>0\); and set \(h(u)=\tfrac12\lVert u\rVert_2^2\) and \(z=x-\eta g\). The Euclidean mirror subproblem is
\[
P_C(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\tfrac12\lVert u-z\rVert_2^2.
\]
For a nonempty box \(C=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,r_i]\), where \(\ell_i\leq r_i\),
\[
(P_C(z))_i=\min\{r_i,\max\{\ell_i,z_i\}\}.
\]
For a nonempty affine set \(C=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:Au=b\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\) has full row rank and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\),
\[
P_C(z)=z-A^{\mathsf T}(AA^{\mathsf T})^{-1}(Az-b).
\]
Both interfaces avoid an iterative projection subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With Euclidean geometry, projection onto a box is coordinatewise clipping, while projection onto a nonempty affine set defined by a full-row-rank matrix is given by an explicit linear-system formula.
assumptions_latex: For the affine formula, \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\) has full row rank and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(z)\) is given by the displayed explicit formula for either specified feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Bregman-Projection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of a Bregman projection over product constraints and separable distance generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(j=1,\ldots,m\), let \(E_j\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(C_j\subseteq E_j\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(h_j:E_j\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Set \(E=E_1\times\cdots\times E_m\), \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), and \(h(u)=\sum_{j=1}^m h_j(u_j)\). Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in C\) with every \(h_j\) differentiable at \(x_j\), let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in E\), and let \(\eta>0\). Then
\[
D_h(u,x)=\sum_{j=1}^m D_{h_j}(u_j,x_j),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\left\{\eta\langle g,u\rangle+D_h(u,x)\right\}
=
\prod_{j=1}^m\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in C_j}\left\{\eta\langle g_j,v\rangle+D_{h_j}(v,x_j)\right\}.
\]
Thus the global Bregman-projection interface factorizes into independent block interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On finite-dimensional product spaces, a separable distance generator and product feasible set factor the Bregman projection into independent block projections.
assumptions_latex: Each \(E_j\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and each \(C_j\subseteq E_j\) is nonempty and convex.
Each \(h_j\) is proper and convex and is differentiable at \(x_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global mirror-subproblem argmin set is the Cartesian product of the \(m\) block argmin sets.

notation.meaning: feasible set in block space E_j

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Inner-Solve Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A function-value accuracy contract for approximately solving a mirror or Bregman subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x\), \(g\), and \(\eta>0\), define
\[
\Phi_x(u)=\eta\langle g,u\rangle+D_h(u,x),\qquad u\in C.
\]
An inner solver is a \(\delta\)-accurate Bregman-projection interface if it returns \(y\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) satisfying
\[
\Phi_x(y)\leq\inf_{u\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}\Phi_x(u)+\delta,
\qquad \delta\geq0.
\]
The exact mirror interface is recovered when \(\delta=0\) and the infimum is attained. For an iterative outer method, the interface reports both \(y_k\) and a certified tolerance \(\delta_k\), allowing convergence conditions to be stated in terms of the accumulated inner errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate mirror subproblem is accepted when its objective value is within a reported nonnegative tolerance of the exact infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned point \(y\) has mirror-subproblem objective gap at most \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: mirror subproblem objective based at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective-gap condition is mathematically coherent and the condition kind fits, but no source is supplied for this particular inexactness interface or for the claim about accumulated outer-method errors. A locator distinguishing objective-gap and residual-based criteria is required.

children.title: Numerical Geometry Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Scaling, domain handling, and coordinate choices affecting numerical realization.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Scaling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal metric scaling for coordinate-sensitive projected and mirror updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex; let \(x\in C\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\eta>0\); and let \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,ldots,d_n)\) with \(d_i>0\). Define \(h_D(v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Dv\) and \(\lVert v\rVert_D^2=v^{\mathsf T}Dv\). Then
\[
D_{h_D}(u,x)=\tfrac12\lVert u-x\rVert_D^2,
\]
and the scaled mirror step satisfies
\[
x^+=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\left\{\eta\langle g,u\rangle+	frac12\lVert u-x\rVert_D^2\right\}
=P_C^D(x-\eta D^{-1}g),
\]
where
\[
P_C^D(z)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in C}\lVert u-z\rVert_D^2.
\]
If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(x_i^+=x_i-\eta g_i/d_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal metric rescales every subgradient coordinate and replaces Euclidean projection by projection in the corresponding weighted norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled mirror update is the \(D\)-metric projection of \(x-\eta D^{-1}g\).

notation.meaning: weighted norm defined by squared norm v-transpose-D-v
projection onto C in the D metric

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Generator Conditioning Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided curvature bounds controlling the numerical geometry induced by a distance generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed space, and let \(h\) be differentiable on \(Q\). For constants \(0<\mu\leq L<\infty\), a \((\mu,L)\)-conditioned distance-generator interface requires that, for all \(x,y\in Q\),
\[
\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2
\leq D_h(y,x)
=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle
\leq\frac{L}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2.
\]
The lower bound supplies strong convexity and therefore uniqueness of any attained minimizer of a convex mirror subproblem, while the upper bound limits curvature amplification. The ratio \(\kappa_h=L/\mu\) is the conditioning parameter of the generator on \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditioned distance generator has Bregman divergence bounded above and below by fixed multiples of squared norm distance; the lower bound ensures uniqueness of an attained convex mirror-subproblem minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h\) is quadratically equivalent to \(\lVert y-x\rVert^2\) on \(Q\), with conditioning ratio \(\kappa_h=L/\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror-Domain Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance conditions preventing mirror iterations from evaluating the generator outside its differentiability domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) and suppose the mirror update requires \(\nabla h(x_k)\). A domain-safe interface initializes \(x_0\in C\cap U\) and accepts a trial point \(y_k\) only if
\[
y_k\in C\cap U,\qquad h(y_k)<\infty,
\qquad \nabla h(y_k)\text{ exists and is finite}.
\]
If any test fails, the interface reduces the trial step size or resolves the subproblem with an interior restriction until the conditions hold. Inductively, every accepted iterate belongs to \(C\cap U\), so the next Bregman divergence and mirror-gradient evaluation are defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize and accept iterates only inside the generator's differentiability domain; otherwise shrink the step or enforce an interior restriction.
assumptions_latex: The mirror implementation evaluates \(h\) and \(\nabla h\) at accepted iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted \(x_k\) lies in \(C\cap U\), keeping subsequent mirror evaluations well-defined.

notation.meaning: interior of the effective domain of h

children.title: Subgradient Trajectory Failures
children.top_down_role: Trajectory behavior that prevents a naive descent or last-iterate interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Descent Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional convex example where a valid subgradient step increases the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f(x)=|x|\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the subgradient iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha g_k\), and a point \(x_k>0\). The unique subgradient there is \(g_k=1\). If \(\alpha>2x_k\), then
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha<0,
\qquad f(x_{k+1})=\alpha-x_k>x_k=f(x_k).
\]
Thus even for a convex Lipschitz objective and an exact subgradient, a legitimate subgradient step need not be a descent step. Convergence analyses based on distance inequalities or best/averaged iterates therefore cannot generally assume monotonic objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the absolute-value objective, a step larger than twice the current positive iterate crosses zero and strictly increases the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_{k+1})>f(x_k)\) for a valid exact subgradient update.

notation.meaning: selected subgradient at the current iterate

source_refs.locator: 8.1 From Gradient Descent to Subgradient Descent p. 195

knowledge_statements.title: Oscillation Near Nonsmooth Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constant-step subgradient orbit cycling across a nonsmooth minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=|x|\), choose a constant step \(\alpha>0\), and initialize \(x_0\in(0,\alpha)\). Since the subgradient is unique away from zero, \(g(x)=1\) for \(x>0\) and \(g(x)=-1\) for \(x<0\). Hence
\[
x_1=x_0-\alpha<0,
\qquad x_2=x_1+\alpha=x_0,
\]
and consequently \(x_{2j}=x_0\) and \(x_{2j+1}=x_0-\alpha\) for every \(j\geq0\). Unless an iterate equals zero, the sequence cycles across the unique minimizer and does not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-step subgradient descent on absolute value alternates forever between two points on opposite sides of the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates form a nonconvergent two-cycle straddling \(x^*=0\).

notation.meaning: the unique minimizer, equal to zero

knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex example where the final subgradient iterate is worse than an earlier iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=|x|\), choose \(\alpha>0\) and \(x_0=\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon<\alpha/2\). Constant-step subgradient descent gives \(x_1=\varepsilon-\alpha\), so
\[
f(x_0)=\varepsilon,
\qquad f(x_1)=\alpha-\varepsilon>\varepsilon.
\]
The subsequent iterates alternate between these points. Therefore, for every odd horizon \(T\), the last iterate satisfies \(f(x_T)=\alpha-\varepsilon\), whereas the best previous value is \(\min_{0\leq k\leq T}f(x_k)=\varepsilon\). A guarantee for a best or averaged iterate does not by itself provide the same guarantee for the last iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-step absolute-value example has odd last iterates much worse than the best earlier iterate, despite a bounded two-cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_T)=\alpha-\varepsilon>\min_{0\leq k\leq T}f(x_k)=\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: positive initial displacement from the minimizer

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient-Selection Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Different valid subgradient selections at one nonsmooth point produce incompatible trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\) and initialize the iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha g_k\) at its minimizer \(x_0=0\), where \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\). The valid selection \(g_0=0\) yields \(x_1=0\) and permits the trajectory to remain optimal. The equally valid selection \(g_0=1\) yields \(x_1=-\alpha\) and \(f(x_1)=\alpha>0=f(x_0)\). Thus the objective and starting point do not determine a unique subgradient trajectory; oracle tie-breaking can determine whether the method stays at or departs from a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the kink of absolute value, selecting zero keeps the iterate optimal, while selecting another valid subgradient moves it away.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Two valid choices from \(\partial f(0)\) produce different next iterates and objective values.

children.title: Stepsize-Target Calibration Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by persistent, prematurely decaying, or miscalibrated policies.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Stepsize Error Floor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent accuracy limitation of projected subgradient descent with a fixed positive step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). Choose \(x_0\in C\), a constant \(\alpha>0\), and subgradients \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) satisfying \(\lVert g_k\rVert_2\leq G\). For the projected subgradient iteration \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k)\), every integer \(T\geq1\) satisfies
\[
\min_{0\leq k<T}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr)
\leq
\frac{\lVert x_0-x^*\rVert_2^2}{2\alpha T}
+rac{\alpha G^2}{2}.
\]
Consequently, this fixed-step guarantee approaches the nonzero scale \(\alpha G^2/2\). For \(C=\mathbb{R}\), \(f(x)=G|x|\), and \(x_0=\alpha G/2\), the iterates form the two-cycle \(\{\alpha G/2,-\alpha G/2\}\), and every iterate has objective error \(\alpha G^2/2\). Thus a fixed positive step does not generally guarantee convergence of the objective error to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected subgradient descent with a fixed positive step has a standard best-iterate bound containing a nonvanishing step-size term, and a scaled absolute-value example attains that error scale at every iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard fixed-step bound has limiting scale \(\alpha G^2/2\), and zero objective error is not guaranteed.

source_refs.locator: 8.1 From Gradient Descent to Subgradient Descent p. 195

source_witnesses.locator: 8.1 From Gradient Descent to Subgradient Descent p. 195

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Stepsize Decay
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summable positive steps can exhaust all motion before reaching a nonsmooth minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(f(x)=|x|\) and positive step sizes satisfying \(S=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k<\infty\). Choose \(x_0>S\). Because every iterate remains positive, the unique subgradient is \(g_k=1\), and
\[
x_k=x_0-\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\alpha_i>x_0-S>0.
\]
Consequently, \(x_k\to x_0-S>0\) and \(f(x_k)\to x_0-S>f(0)=0\). Thus decay fast enough to make the total step length finite can prevent convergence even for a one-dimensional convex Lipschitz objective with exact subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If positive step sizes are summable, absolute-value descent can use all available motion yet stop strictly before the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates converge to \(x_0-S>0\), not to the minimizer \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Incorrect Polyak Targets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Overestimating the optimal value in the Polyak stepsize can create a nonoptimal fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)=|x|\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), whose optimal value is \(f^*=0\). For \(x_k\ne0\), choose \(g_k=\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\) and apply the Polyak rule with an incorrect target \(\tau>f^*\): \[\alpha_k=\frac{f(x_k)-\tau}{\lVert g_k\rVert^2},\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k.\] Then \(x_{k+1}=\tau\operatorname{sign}(x_k)\). Hence every initialization \(x_0\ne0\) reaches \(\tau\operatorname{sign}(x_0)\) in one step and remains there, with \(f(x_k)-f^*=\tau\). Thus replacing the true optimal value by an overestimate destroys convergence to optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the absolute-value objective, an overestimated Polyak target makes the method stop at objective error equal to the target error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k=\tau\operatorname{sign}(x_0)\) and \(f(x_k)-f^*=\tau\) for every \(k\ge1\).

notation.meaning: Incorrect estimate of the optimal objective value
Selected subgradient at the current iterate

children.title: Unknown-Scale Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Policy failures caused by unavailable or misestimated objective, oracle, or domain scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Scale Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stepsize calibrated with the wrong subgradient scale incurs a multiplicative scale-mismatch penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\). Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, assume \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and write \(f^*=f(x^*)\). For \(T\ge1\), run \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k)\), where \(x_0\in C\), \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\lVert g_k\rVert\le G\), \(G>0\), and \(\alpha=D/(\widehat G\sqrt{T})\) for an estimate \(\widehat G>0\). With \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}x_k\), \[f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le\frac{D}{2\sqrt{T}}\left(\widehat G+\frac{G^2}{\widehat G}\right).\] Relative to \(DG/\sqrt{T}\), the right-hand side has factor \((\widehat G/G+G/\widehat G)/2\), which is unbounded under arbitrary scale mismatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using an incorrect positive subgradient-norm scale preserves the standard rate certificate only up to a factor that grows without bound in either direction of scale mismatch.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le D(\widehat G+G^2/\widehat G)/(2\sqrt{T})\).

notation.meaning: Scale used to calibrate the stepsize

children.title: Unknown-Horizon Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Policy failures caused by unavailable or changing termination horizons.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Horizon Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A constant stepsize tuned to a planned horizon may cease providing a decreasing certificate when execution exceeds that horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\). Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, assume \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and write \(f^*=f(x^*)\). Starting from \(x_0\in C\), run \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha g_k)\), where \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(\lVert g_k\rVert\le G\), \(G>0\), and \(\alpha=D/(G\sqrt{\widehat T})\) for a planned horizon \(\widehat T\ge1\). For an actual runtime \(T\ge1\) and \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}x_k\), \[f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le\frac{DG}{2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{\widehat T}}{T}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\widehat T}}\right).\] The terms balance when \(\widehat T=T\). If \(\widehat T\) is fixed while \(T\to\infty\), this certificate approaches \(DG/(2\sqrt{\widehat T})\), so it does not certify continued convergence to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant stepsize selected for a fixed planned horizon leaves a positive asymptotic error certificate when the method is run indefinitely beyond that horizon.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le (DG/2)(\sqrt{\widehat T}/T+1/\sqrt{\widehat T})\).

notation.meaning: Planned horizon used to select the constant stepsize
Uniform average of the first T iterates

children.title: Scale–Horizon Calibration Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interaction between scale adaptation, horizon dependence, and phase-based policy repair.

knowledge_statements.title: Scale–Horizon Calibration Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a family of scale-and-horizon-tuned constant stepsizes retains the canonical projected-subgradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\). Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, assume \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and write \(f^*=f(x^*)\). Assume selected subgradients satisfy \(\lVert g_k\rVert\le G\) for some \(G>0\). For each runtime \(T\ge1\), choose \(\widehat G_T>0\) and \(\widehat T_T\ge1\), and run \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_Tg_k)\) for \(T\) steps from \(x_0\in C\), with \(\alpha_T=D/(\widehat G_T\sqrt{\widehat T_T})\). For \(\bar x_T=T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}x_k\), \[f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le\frac{D\widehat G_T\sqrt{\widehat T_T}}{2T}+\frac{DG^2}{2\widehat G_T\sqrt{\widehat T_T}}.\] Define \(r_T=\widehat G_T\sqrt{\widehat T_T}/(G\sqrt{T})\). The displayed right-hand side divided by \(DG/\sqrt{T}\) equals \((r_T+r_T^{-1})/2\). Consequently, this family of certificates is uniformly \(O(DG/\sqrt{T})\) if and only if \(r_T\) is bounded above and bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical certificate is retained exactly when the estimated scale times the square root of the planned horizon remains comparable to the true scale times the square root of the actual runtime.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed certificate is uniformly \(O(DG/\sqrt{T})\) if and only if \(0<\inf_{T\ge1}r_T\le\sup_{T\ge1}r_T<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Combined scale–horizon calibration ratio at runtime T
Estimated subgradient scale used for the T-step run
Planned horizon used for the T-step run

children.title: Oracle-Domain Well-Posedness Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures of oracle regularity, feasible geometry, or subproblem well-posedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Oracle Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded subgradients can make a fixed-step first-order iteration expansive far from the solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize the convex differentiable function \(f(x)=x^4\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) by the fixed-step update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha g_k\), where \(g_k=4x_k^3\) and \(\alpha>0\). Then \[|x_{k+1}|=|x_k|\,|1-4\alpha x_k^2|.\] Whenever \(|x_k|>1/\sqrt{2\alpha}\), the multiplier is greater than one, so \(|x_{k+1}|>|x_k|\). The same inequality then persists, and the iterate magnitudes grow without bound. Thus convexity alone, without a bounded-oracle region or an adaptive stepsize safeguard, does not make a global fixed-step subgradient iteration stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex quartic objective, sufficiently large initial points make fixed-step gradient iterates grow because the oracle magnitude is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|x_{k+1}|>|x_k|\) for all \(k\), and \(|x_k|\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: Exact first-order oracle value at the current iterate

children.title: Biased Oracle Error
children.top_down_role: Systematic directional or value distortion in oracle information.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Oracle Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonzero mean oracle bias can shift the limiting point away from the optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with minimizer \(x^*=0\), and suppose the oracle always returns \(\widetilde g_k=x_k+b\) for a fixed bias \(b\ne0\). For a constant stepsize \(0<\alpha<2\), the update is \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\widetilde g_k=(1-\alpha)x_k-\alpha b.\] Consequently \(x_k+b=(1-\alpha)^k(x_0+b)\), so \(x_k\to-b\). The limiting objective error is \(f(-b)-f(x^*)=b^2/2>0\). Hence boundedness of oracle error alone does not ensure convergence to the true solution when the error has persistent bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant additive oracle bias makes gradient descent converge to the zero of the biased oracle, not to the true minimizer.

children.title: Persistent Oracle Error
children.top_down_role: Oracle error that remains nonnegligible across the optimization trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Oracle Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondecaying zero-average-in-time errors can prevent last-iterate convergence through a stable oscillation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\) and use the inexact oracle \(\widetilde g_k=x_k+e_k\), where \(e_k=(-1)^k\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon>0\). For a constant stepsize \(0<\alpha<2\), set \(c=\alpha\varepsilon/(2-\alpha)\) and initialize \(x_0=c\). The recursion \[x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)x_k-\alpha e_k\] then gives \(x_k=(-1)^k c\) for every \(k\). Thus the iterates do not converge, although the error sequence is bounded and has zero Cesàro mean. Their objective values remain at the positive level \(c^2/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded alternating oracle error can sustain a two-cycle, so nondecaying error may defeat last-iterate convergence even without constant bias.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k=(-1)^k\alpha\varepsilon/(2-\alpha)\) and \(f(x_k)=\alpha^2\varepsilon^2/[2(2-\alpha)^2]\).

source_refs.locator: 8 Primal and Dual Projected Subgradient Methods p. 195

children.title: Oracle Error Decay Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation between vanishing-error regimes and persistent-error regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Error Decay Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The averaged projected-subgradient certificate depends on the stepsize-weighted average of the inexact-subgradient errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\). Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, assume \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and write \(f^*=f(x^*)\). Starting from \(x_0\in C\), run \(x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k\widetilde g_k)\), where \(\alpha_k>0\), \(\lVert\widetilde g_k\rVert\le G\), and \(\widetilde g_k\) satisfies \(f(y)\ge f(x_k)+\langle\widetilde g_k,y-x_k\rangle-\delta_k\) for every \(y\in C\), with \(\delta_k\ge0\). Define \(S_T=\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k\) and \(\bar x_T=S_T^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_kx_k\). Then \[f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le\frac{D^2+G^2\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k^2}{2S_T}+\frac{\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k\delta_k}{S_T}.\] Hence this certificate converges to zero if \(S_T\to\infty\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k^2/S_T\to0\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k\delta_k/S_T\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For projected inexact-subgradient descent, the displayed averaged-iterate certificate vanishes when the cumulative stepsize diverges, its quadratic contribution is negligible, and the stepsize-weighted average oracle error tends to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{diam}(C)\le D<\infty\)
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and attains its minimum on \(C\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(S_T\to\infty\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k^2/S_T\to0\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}\alpha_k\delta_k/S_T\to0\), then \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\to0\).

notation.meaning: Cumulative stepsize through the first T iterations
Stepsize-weighted average of the first T iterates

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Unbounded Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Without coercivity, a bounded solution set, or another growth control, an unbounded domain may admit no optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb{R}\) and minimize the convex function \(f(x)=-x\). Its subdifferential is \(\partial f(x)=\{-1\}\), but \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=-\infty\), so no minimizer \(x^*\) exists. For any positive stepsizes \(\alpha_k\), the unprojected subgradient iteration satisfies \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k(-1)=x_k+\alpha_k.\] If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), then \(x_k\to+\infty\) and \(f(x_k)\to-\infty\). Thus the usual distance-to-solution and finite optimality-gap guarantees are not even well-defined on an uncontrolled unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective on the real line has no minimizer, so subgradient iterates escape and standard solution-distance guarantees are undefined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to+\infty\), \(f(x_k)\to-\infty\), and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)=\varnothing\).

children.title: Ill-Posed Projection Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Projection failures involving missing solutions, nonunique outputs, or unstable access.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Posed Projection Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of closedness can make the Euclidean projection infimum unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(z=2\). The Euclidean projection subproblem is \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12|x-z|^2.\] Its infimum equals \(1/2\), approached as \(x\uparrow1\), but no point of \(C\) attains it. Hence \(P_C(2)=\varnothing\), even though \(C\) is nonempty and convex. A projected subgradient or mirror-prox update requiring this projection is therefore undefined. The example isolates closedness as an essential existence assumption for the standard projection theorem on closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto the open interval can fail because the nearest boundary point is excluded, leaving the algorithmic update undefined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12|x-z|^2=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Set of Euclidean projections of z onto C

children.title: Ill-Posed Proximal Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Generalized prox failures involving solvability, uniqueness, coercivity, or numerical stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Posed Proximal Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A proper convex but nonclosed function can have a proximal infimum that is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the proper convex function \(h:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(h(0)=1\), \(h(x)=0\) for \(x>0\), and \(h(x)=+\infty\) for \(x<0\). The function is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\). For \(z=-1\) and \(\lambda>0\), consider \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{h(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}|x-z|^2\right\}.\] Values with \(x>0\) approach \(1/(2\lambda)\) as \(x\downarrow0\), while the value at \(0\) is \(1+1/(2\lambda)\). Thus the infimum is not attained and the proximal mapping is empty at \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function lacking lower semicontinuity can have an unattained proximal infimum, so its proximal update need not exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(z)=\varnothing\).

children.title: Subproblem Solvability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Domain, geometry, and regularization regimes separating well-posed from ill-posed subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Subproblem Solvability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard closed-convex hypotheses make Euclidean projection and convex proximal subproblems uniquely solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. If \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then for every \(z\in H\) the problem \[\min_{x\in C}\frac12\lVert x-z\rVert^2\] has a unique solution \(P_C(z)\). If \(h:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, then for every \(z\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\), \[\min_{x\in H}\left\{h(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert x-z\rVert^2\right\}\] likewise has a unique solution \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(z)\). Consequently, algorithms invoking these exact subproblems have single-valued updates under these hypotheses; dropping closedness or lower semicontinuity can destroy existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty closed convex sets and proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions yield unique projection and proximal updates; weaker data may not.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex
\(h\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(z)\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(z)\) exist uniquely for every \(z\in H\) and \(\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of h with parameter lambda

children.title: Mirror-Geometry Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by an incompatible or computationally unsuitable distance generator.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry–Domain Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate failure when mirror geometry does not control the feasible domain and oracle in dual norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(h\) be differentiable on the iterates, and define \(D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\). Standard mirror-descent bounds require finite constants \(R^2\ge \sup_{x\in C}D_h(x,x_1)\) and \(G\ge \sup_t\lVert g_t\rVert_*\), with \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\), in the norm relative to which \(h\) is strongly convex. If either constant is infinite or unavailable because the geometry is incompatible with \(C\) or the oracle, the usual bound \(RG/\sqrt{T}\) is vacuous; mirror descent may remain defined, but that geometry supplies no finite worst-case guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-descent rates become vacuous when the chosen Bregman geometry has infinite domain radius or fails to bound subgradients in its dual norm.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex, and all iterates lie where \(h\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=\infty\) or \(G=\infty\) implies that the standard \(RG/\sqrt{T}\) guarantee gives no finite error bound.

notation.meaning: Bregman radius of the feasible domain from the initial point

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Singularity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Legendre-type mirror maps whose gradients are undefined or divergent on the feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the probability simplex \(\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\sum_i x_i=1\}\), take the negative-entropy generator \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\), with \(0\log 0=0\). Although \(h\) is finite on \(\Delta_n\), its gradient satisfies \((\nabla h(x))_i=1+\log x_i\) only when every \(x_i>0\). Hence a mirror update written through \(\nabla h(x_t)\), or its inverse, is not classically defined when an iterate has a zero coordinate. An algorithm using this representation must initialize and remain in \(\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\), or replace the gradient formula by a boundary-compatible generalized proximal formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is finite on the simplex boundary, but its gradient is not; gradient-based mirror coordinates therefore fail at zero coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 2\) and the mirror generator is negative entropy on \(\Delta_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t,i}=0\) for some \(i\) implies that \(\nabla h(x_t)\) is not a finite vector, so the classical dual-coordinate update is undefined.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Distance Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of iterate control when the Bregman generator lacks strict or strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and convex. If \(h\) is affine on a nontrivial segment, then distinct points \(x\ne y\) on that segment satisfy \(D_h(x,y)=0\). Consequently the mirror subproblem \(\min_{x\in C}\{\eta\langle g,x\rangle+D_h(x,y)\}\) has no Bregman penalty along that segment and may be nonunique or make an uncontrolled displacement. In the extreme case \(h\equiv0\), \(D_h\equiv0\), so the subproblem reduces to linear minimization. Thus convexity of \(h\) alone cannot provide the quadratic lower bound needed for standard mirror-descent stability and rate analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the generator is affine in feasible directions, distinct points can have zero Bregman distance, eliminating the stabilization used by mirror descent.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) contains a nontrivial segment on which \(h\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(x\ne y\) with \(D_h(x,y)=0\), so no positive strong-convexity modulus controls displacement on \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Mirror-Map Inversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bounds do not imply efficiency when the mirror inverse or Bregman proximal map is costly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dual-coordinate mirror step has the form \(z_{t+1}=\nabla h(x_t)-\eta_t g_t\) followed by \(x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in C}\{\langle-z_{t+1},x\rangle+h(x)\}\), which equals \((\nabla h)^{-1}(z_{t+1})\) only in an unconstrained Legendre setting. If evaluating this inverse or solving the constrained Bregman proximal problem costs \(M\) elementary operations, then \(T\) mirror iterations cost at least \(T M\), aside from oracle work. Therefore an oracle-complexity bound counting only subgradient evaluations does not establish computational advantage when \(M\) is large, unavailable in closed form, or itself requires a high-accuracy iterative solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A favorable iteration count can conceal prohibitive work when each step requires an expensive inverse mirror map or Bregman proximal solve.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a mirror generator for which the displayed subproblem has a solution.
\(M\) denotes the per-iteration cost of computing that solution to the required accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The arithmetic work is at least \(T M\), so a bound of \(T\) oracle calls alone does not bound practical runtime independently of the mirror implementation.

notation.meaning: cost of one mirror inversion or Bregman proximal solve

knowledge_statements.title: Unstabilized Dynamic Mirror Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional counterexample showing failure under uncontrolled time-varying mirror scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[0,1]\), \(f(x)=x\), \(x_1=1\), and choose dynamic generators \(h_t(x)=a_t x^2/2\) with \(a_t>0\). For fixed \(\eta>0\), the dynamic mirror step is \(x_{t+1}=\max\{0,x_t-\eta/a_t\}\). If \(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta/a_t<1\), then \(x_t=1-\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\eta/a_s\) remains positive and converges to a nonoptimal limit, although every \(h_t\) is strongly convex. Thus per-iteration strong convexity is insufficient: uncontrolled growth of mirror curvature can make the effective steps summable and prevent convergence to the minimizer \(x^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rapidly increasing mirror curvature can make effective steps summable, causing convergence to a nonoptimal point even though every generator is strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\to 1-\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\eta/a_t>0=x^*\), so the dynamic mirror iteration fails to converge to the minimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient-to-Bundle Stabilization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural transition from a single current subgradient to a stabilized multi-cut model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex \(f\), a plain subgradient step uses only \((f(x_t),g_t)\), where \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). A bundle method begins when stored oracle pairs \((x_i,f(x_i),g_i)\) define the cutting-plane model \(m_t(x)=\max_{i\in I_t}\{f(x_i)+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\}\), and the next trial point minimizes a stabilized model such as \(m_t(x)+(2\lambda_t)^{-1}\lVert x-c_t\rVert^2\). The memory set \(I_t\), proximal center \(c_t\), and serious/null-step acceptance logic are additional algorithmic state. Without stabilization, minimizing the polyhedral model can be unbounded or produce arbitrarily remote trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bundle boundary is crossed when stored supporting cuts form a model whose minimization is stabilized and governed by serious/null-step logic.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex, and each stored \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\).
\(\lambda_t>0\) and \(I_t\) is a finite nonempty index set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Use of \(m_t\), a stabilization term, and bundle-management state defines a bundle method rather than a memoryless subgradient iteration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record accurately describes the structural transition from a memoryless subgradient step to a stabilized cutting-plane bundle model, and failure_boundary fits the terminal boundary container. No citation is supplied for the bundle model, stabilization, serious/null-step state, or the unstabilized-model failure claim, so an authoritative bundle-method section or theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient-to-Proximal Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition caused by treating a nonsmooth component through its proximal map rather than a selected subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=f(x)+r(x)\) on a closed convex set \(C\). A projected subgradient step on the full objective selects \(s_t\in\partial F(x_t)\) and projects \(x_t-\eta_t s_t\). The proximal boundary is crossed when \(r\) is retained exactly in the update \(x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in C}\{\langle g_t,x\rangle+r(x)+(2\eta_t)^{-1}\lVert x-x_t\rVert^2\}\), with \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). If \(f\) is differentiable and \(g_t=\nabla f(x_t)\), this is proximal gradient; for nonsmooth \(f\), it is a proximal-subgradient step. The transition is meaningful only when this proximal subproblem is computationally accessible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method becomes proximal when one nonsmooth component is kept intact in a tractable proximal subproblem instead of being replaced by a subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(r\) are proper convex functions on \(C\).
\(\eta_t>0\), and the displayed proximal subproblem has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact inclusion of \(r\) in the regularized subproblem separates proximal-family updates from full-objective projected subgradient steps.

notation.meaning: component handled by a proximal operation
subgradient or gradient of the forward component

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror-Descent-to-Mirror-Prox Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition from one-point mirror descent to an extragradient correction for monotone variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be closed and convex, let \(F:C\to X^*\) be monotone, and let \(h\) generate \(D_h\). A mirror-descent step evaluates \(F(x_t)\) once and sets \(x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in C}\{\eta_t\langle F(x_t),x\rangle+D_h(x,x_t)\}\). Mirror-Prox begins when a predictor \(y_t\) is computed by this rule and a corrected point is formed using a second evaluation: \(x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in C}\{\eta_t\langle F(y_t),x\rangle+D_h(x,x_t)\}\). The extra evaluation is substantive for general monotone Lipschitz operators, where one-point descent need not provide the corrected variational-inequality progress estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-Prox starts when a predictor is followed by a second operator evaluation and a correction from the original mirror center.
assumptions_latex: The two displayed Bregman proximal subproblems are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(F(x_t)\) by the predictor evaluation \(F(y_t)\) in a second centered step crosses from mirror descent to Mirror-Prox.

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence used by both steps

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-to-Conditional-Gradient Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Substitution of a linear minimization oracle for projection changes both the update and admissible objective model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable convex \(f\) on compact convex \(C\), projected gradient computes \(P_C(x_t-\eta_t
abla f(x_t))\). The conditional-gradient boundary is crossed by calling the linear minimization oracle \(s_t\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle
abla f(x_t),sangle\) and setting \(x_{t+1}=(1-\gamma_t)x_t+\gamma_t s_t\). This removes projection but requires a tractable linear oracle and preserves feasibility by convex combination. For a merely nonsmooth objective, replacing \(
abla f(x_t)\) with an arbitrary subgradient does not inherit the standard smooth conditional-gradient descent estimate, because that estimate depends on a curvature or smoothness upper model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional gradient replaces projection by linear minimization and convex averaging, but its standard guarantee requires smooth curvature control absent from arbitrary subgradient oracles.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and convex on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear-oracle update is projection-free, while the usual conditional-gradient analysis does not follow for unrestricted nonsmooth subgradients.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projected-gradient and conditional-gradient updates are stated consistently, and the warning that arbitrary nonsmooth subgradients do not inherit the standard smooth conditional-gradient estimate is mathematically appropriate. The failure_boundary kind fits the transition leaf, but no source supports either the method boundary or the smoothness/curvature limitation. A direct conditional-gradient source locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman-to-Splitting Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition from one composite Bregman subproblem to separate operator evaluations for structured inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the inclusion \(0\in A(x)+B(x)\), where \(A\) and \(B\) are monotone operators. A single Bregman proximal step for the combined operator would require the resolvent-like map associated with \(A+B\). The splitting boundary is crossed when an iteration evaluates \(A\) and \(B\) through separate explicit, resolvent, or Bregman-resolvent operations whose composition has the same fixed-point solutions. This distinction is computational: separate resolvents may be tractable even when the resolvent of \(A+B\) is not. If no monotonicity, averagedness, cocoercivity, or compatible step-size condition controls the chosen composition, separate evaluation alone does not guarantee convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman iteration becomes an operator-splitting method when structured terms are processed by separate maps whose fixed points solve the original inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) act on a common finite-dimensional space.
The zero set \(\{x:0\in A(x)+B(x)\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate processing of \(A\) and \(B\) crosses the splitting boundary only when the composed map preserves the solution set and satisfies a convergence-enabling regularity condition.

notation.meaning: sum operator defining the target inclusion
